item.description:
URL: https://garymarcus.substack.com/p/breaking-eli-lilly-ceo-becomes-latest, See on Hacker News

Moments after I posted my essay on why I couldn’t touch Anthropic’s IPO with a ten-foot pole, Anthropic’s CEO gave me (and everyone else) a reason to run away as fast as possible: a video tied to the IPO launch in which he made a bunch of overpromise about medicine that would have made Elizabeth Holmes blush.

NIK@ns123abc

Anthropic CEO predicts cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, mental illness will be cured in less than 10 years ACCELERATE

7:12 PM · Nov 10, 2026 · 2.45M Views

1.29K Replies · 1.06K Reposts · 13.3K Likes

As I have discussed before, this is not going to happen on anything remotely like that timeline. Cancer is more than one thing, and it will take more than a decade to eradicate it; the bit about curing mental illness (and some other things) that quickly is absolute fantasy.

The response from experts on X has been swift, and absolutely (and appropriately) brutal.

I was hardly the only one to get serious Elizabeth Holmes vibes. Here are four of my favorites:

Geoff Shullenberger@g_shullenberger

If you can’t see at least some parallels with Elizabeth Holmes here I don’t know what to tell you…

NIK @ns123abc

Anthropic CEO predicts cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, mental illness will be cured in less than 10 years ACCELERATE

2:48 PM · Nov 11, 2026 · 123K Views

202 Replies · 897 Reposts · 8.88K Likes

9:42 PM · Nov 11, 2026 · 265K Views

104 Replies · 616 Reposts · 16.2K Likes

Alheli Picazo@a_picazo

That's not how mental illness works, and frankly, the more fantastical promises/predictions these CEOs make, the stronger the case against trusting them or their product becomes. Big Elizabeth Holmes/Theranos vibes.

John Cassidy @JohnCassidy

In other news, AI will cure mental illness within a decade.

item.title: The Netherlands Is Dismantling the International Criminal Court (142 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://rightsforum.org/en/diplomatic-sources-the-netherlands-is-negotiating-the-dismantling-of-the-international-criminal-court/, See on Hacker News

Klik hier voor Nederlandse versie

Under pressure from US sanctions against the International Criminal Court, the Netherlands is cooperating in its dismantling, The Rights Forum has learned from reliable sources.

The Netherlands is negotiating with the US over the erosion of the powers of the International Criminal Court (ICC). This erosion is so drastic that, according to legal experts, it would amount to the dismantling of the Court. The Rights Forum has learnt this from diplomatic sources in New York, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The restrictions that would be under discussion include: a) granting immunity to heads of state; b) excluding the Court’s jurisdiction over nationals of non-state parties, even when they commit crimes on the territory of a state party; and c) denying the Court’s jurisdiction over cases covered by national legislation.

First and second restrictions

The first restriction would mean that heads of state and heads of government such as Netanyahu, Trump and Putin could not be prosecuted for crimes committed on their orders.

The second restriction would mean that the ICC could no longer prosecute nationals of non-state parties, even if they commit international crimes on the territory of a state that is a party to the Rome Statute – the founding treaty of the ICC.

Israel, for example, is not a party to the Rome Statute, whereas Palestine is. Consequently, under the current rules, the ICC can prosecute Israeli citizens and government officials for crimes they commit on Palestinian territory. On this basis, the Court has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant.

However, if the second restriction were to be adopted, Israeli nationals could no longer be prosecuted for crimes committed on Palestinian territory. The same would apply to US or Russian nationals who commit crimes on the territory of other States Parties.

This would undermine a key principle of the International Criminal Court: that nationals of states which have not ratified the Rome Statute can also be held accountable for international crimes.

Third restriction

The third restriction would mean that the ICC would no longer be permitted to hear cases if a state has legislation enabling it, in principle, to punish offences committed within its own jurisdiction. At present, the Court may still intervene if a state is unwilling or unable to investigate and prosecute suspects (the so-called principle of complementarity). If the third restriction were introduced, the mere existence of national legislation could be sufficient to prevent prosecution by the ICC.

For example: Israel has legislation against torture. It could therefore argue that the ICC has no jurisdiction, even if, in practice, cases of torture are not investigated or prosecuted. In this way, Israel could avert prosecution by the ICC without taking action against the perpetrators itself.

In short: if the aforementioned restrictions are adopted, there will be nothing left of the Court.

In order to enshrine these legal restrictions, the Rome Statute – which established the International Criminal Court in 1998 and under which it has operated since 2002 – would need to be amended. This would require a two-thirds majority of the States Parties. The amendment must then be ratified by seven-eighths of the States Parties before it can enter into force. It is not known which countries would cooperate in this regard.

US sanctions

The reason the Netherlands is said to be negotiating on this matter are the sanctions imposed by the US against thirteen judges and prosecutors, and against the ICC as a whole. This was done primarily in retaliation for the Court’s investigation into Israeli crimes in Palestine, and the resulting arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant. The undermining of the International Criminal Court by the US and Israel has now been going on for almost twelve years.

The Court has been on the US sanctions list since 9 October. However, a number of sanctions will not come into force until 7 April 2027. These would largely paralyse the institution, leaving the European Union with virtually no choice but to activate the far-reaching blocking mechanism. This law obliges European parties to disregard US sanctions and to continue supplying services and goods to the Court and its staff.

The EU, and EU countries like the Netherlands, are, however, reluctant to activate the mechanism due to the consequences it could have for European businesses. For instance, European banks that disregard the US sanctions might find it much more difficult to do business in the US – or could face sanctions themselves.

Opting for a compromise

That is why the Netherlands now appears to be opting for a compromise. By relinquishing certain aspects of the International Criminal Court, the US might be persuaded to lift or ease the sanctions against the Court. In practice, this would amount to amputating the Court’s limbs. What would then remain is a powerless trunk-court.

We are not quite there yet. The States Parties to the Rome Statute will meet in The Hague from 30 November to 7 December. The meeting was originally scheduled to take place in New York, but the US sanctions made it necessary to relocate it.

Response from the ministry of Foreign Affairs

The Rights Forum has asked the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for a response to the reports, but it provides a general, meaningless statement and does not address the specific questions asked:

‘At the previous Meeting of States Parties (in December 2025), it was decided by consensus to encourage States Parties to engage in further dialogue with non-States Parties. In the run-up to the forthcoming Meeting of States Parties to the Rome Statute (30 November – 7 December), States Parties are continuing discussions on this matter and we are exploring the scope for dialogue with non-States Parties, within the framework of international law and with due regard for the independence and impartiality of the Court.

‘We cannot yet anticipate how such a dialogue will unfold, as this is not solely up to us: the Netherlands, together with the other 124 States Parties and our European partners, bears a shared responsibility to protect the Court. No concrete proposals are currently before the Assembly of States Parties.

‘In any case, we remain firmly committed to the Court and will continue to do our utmost to ensure it functions effectively: both as the host country and as a State Party. Independent courts and tribunals must be able to carry out their mandates unhindered. In these capacities, we also remain fully committed – together with other States Parties – to mitigating the impact of existing sanctions. It is important that the Court is able to function as freely as possible.’

item.title: IceWM (272 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ice-wm.org/, See on Hacker News

IceWM is a window manager for the X Window System. The goal of IceWM is speed, simplicity, and not getting in the user’s way. It comes with a taskbar with pager, global and per-window keybindings and a dynamic menu system. Application windows can be managed by keyboard and mouse. Windows can be iconified to the taskbar, to the tray, to the desktop or be made hidden. They are controllable by a quick switch window (Alt+Tab) and in a window list. A handful of configurable focus models are menu-selectable. Setups with multiple monitors are supported by RandR and Xinerama. IceWM is very configurable, themeable and well documented. It includes an optional external background wallpaper manager with transparency support, a simple session manager and a system tray. IceWM is available on popular Linux distributions like Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, OpenSUSE, Gentoo, Slackware, CentOS, antiX, NixOS and on most *BSDs.

Software

IceWM was created by Marko Maček in 1997 using C++. It is now maintained at Github.

Releases

The latest released version is 4.1.0 (2026-08-06).

Features

  • Easy to use, simple and fast
  • Standards compliant→
  • Fully usable with keyboard
  • Alt+Tab window switching
  • Efficient resource usage
  • Task bar (optional)
  • Multiple workspaces
  • Fully documented→
  • A large number of themes→
  • Usable with GNOME and KDE environments
  • Regenerates menus when configuration changes
  • Support for sound effects→
  • Multiple focus modes
  • Manual placement of windows option
  • Autoraising of windows option
  • Tooltips
  • Configurable keybindings→
  • Supports DockApps in a container
  • Tabbed windows

Screenshots

The IceWM Screenshots Collection

Themes

IceWM is themeable. The visual appearance of icewm can be changed by a theme, which is a collection of settings and small images. Over 450 themes can be downloaded from box-look.org. Extra is a collection of 91 highlights. See icewm -i list.

Translations

IceWM is translated into three dozen languages. To improve the translation for your language at Weblate, first register an account either here or there, then update.

Documentation

  • IceWM man pages
  • IceWM Manual
  • Themes Howto
  • IceWM FAQ

Bug Tracking

Report your icewm bugs on Github. Only report it once and give relevant details.

Install the latest release as follows

$ wget https://github.com/ice-wm/icewm/releases/download/4.1.0/icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
$ tar -x --lzip -vpf icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
$ cd icewm-4.1.0
$ ./configure --prefix=/usr
$ make
$ sudo make install

Install from unreleased development source code

Gettext must be installed.

$ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
$ cd icewm
$ ./autogen.sh
$ ./configure --prefix=/usr
$ make
$ sudo make install

If you have cmake, an alternative is:

$ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
$ cd icewm
$ ./rebuild.sh -r --prefix=/usr
$ cd build
$ sudo make install

Install package dependencies

To install all package dependencies in one go use the following script.

$ wget https://ice-wm.org/scripts/os-depends.sh
$ sudo bash -x ./os-depends.sh

Verify package dependencies by:

$ pkg-config --modversion x11 xext xcomposite xcursor xdamage xfixes xres xrender xrandr xinerama xft fontconfig sm ice sndfile alsa ao gio-2.0 gio-unix-2.0 gdk-pixbuf-xlib-2.0 imlib2 librsvg-2.0 xpm libpng libjpeg
# or simpler:
$ ./rebuild.sh -d

  • IceWM from scratch.
  • IceWM on arch wiki.
  • IceWM by arch user.

item.title: Switcher (2004) (112 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://folklore.org/Switcher.html, See on Hacker News

The first commercial product that I worked on after going on leave of absence from Apple in March 1984 (see Leave Of Absence) was a low cost, high resolution scanner for the Macintosh called Thunderscan, that I created in collaboration with a tiny company named Thunderware (see Thunderscan). I started working on it in June 1984, and by early October, it was almost complete.

Tom Petrie, one of the two principals at Thunderware (the other was Victor Bull, who I worked with on the Silentype thermal printer (see What Hath Woz Wrought), the first project that I did for Apple), arranged a few demos for various computer magazines, to curry favorable reviews to promote the product. On October 11th, 1984, I drove with Tom to an office in Hillsborough, to demonstrate Thunderscan for Byte magazine.

The Byte reviewer was John Markoff, a technology scribe for the San Francisco Chronicle who was one of the best reporters covering the personal computer industry. Tom described Thunderscan while I set up the demo and started scanning. John asked a few questions, taking notes with his IBM PC, which was running a character-based text editor that I viewed with the typical pious disdain of a Macintosh purist. As I was answering one of his questions, the phone rang.

"Excuse me," he told us, as he pressed a key combination on his keyboard, his monitor screen instantly changing to a different program. He talked on the phone for a minute or two, occasionally typing, before he finished the conversation and pressed a key combination to switch back to his Thunderscan notes.

"What did you just do?," I asked John, curious about the software that he was running. "How did you switch to another application so quickly?"

"Oh, I'm running Memory Shift. Haven't you seen it?" John responded. "It's a DOS utility program that keeps multiple applications resident in memory, and allows you to switch between them quickly. I've been using it a lot lately." John typed the switch command a few times in rapid succession, to show me how fast it could do its thing.

"You know, I think I could do that for the Macintosh", I suddenly blurted out, before I even thought about it consciously.

The 512K Macintosh, with four times the memory of the original, had just started shipping a few weeks ago. I had considered trying to run multiple applications simultaneously on the 512K Mac, but I was stymied by low memory conflicts and other potential gotchas. But now, as I observed Memory Shift in action on John's PC, I suddenly saw a simple way to do it, which didn't seem to be too hard to implement.

"Yeah, that would be cool," John agreed. I continued with the Thunderscan demo, but it was hard for me to concentrate on it, because I couldn't stop thinking about application switching. There were a few intricate problems to solve, but it seemed eminently doable, and I thought it would be incredibly useful if I got it to work.

Tom Petrie noticed how excited I was about the new idea and, as he drove me home from the demo, he reminded me of my prior commitments, and made me promise that I would finish the alpha release of Thunderscan as soon as possible, before daring to start something new. We agreed on a list of a dozen or so tasks, which I thought I could accomplish within two weeks. Once the alpha release was completed, I could take a short hiatus, in order to work on application switching, before diving back into Thunderscan to finish the 1.0 release, due by the end of November.

During the next two weeks, I focused on polishing Thunderscan to get it ready for the alpha release, but I also spent idle moments pondering the design of the application switcher. One fundamental decision was whether or not to load all of the applications into a single heap, which would make optimal use of memory by minimizing fragmentation, or to allocate separate "heap zones" for each application. I decided to opt for separate heap zones to better isolate the applications, but I wasn't sure that was right.

There were lots of little problems to solve. The most crucial one was that the system software kept lots of application-specific global variables in low memory (see Mea Culpa), which needed to be swapped during context switching, so each application could maintain its own set of them. The hard part was coming up with the precise list of exactly what needed to be swapped; many of the variables were obvious, but some were quite subtle, and dependent on how applications were using them. I knew that my first cut wouldn't be perfect, but I was confident that I could debug the inevitable problems once I saw how the applications were actually failing.

A few days after starting the push to finish Thunderscan, I received an intriguing phone call from Jeff Harbers, the manager of Microsoft's Macintosh applications team. Jeff told me that Microsoft had a very strategic project that they needed for the Macintosh, and that they thought that I was the ideal person to implement it. He wouldn't tell me anything else over the phone, but he offered to fly me up to Seattle to discuss it in person. Even though I was right in the middle of trying to complete Thunderscan, I was intrigued enough to accept his offer to fly up to Seattle and visit with him the following Tuesday.

Jeff picked me up at the airport, and we drove to Microsoft's main building where we were joined by Neil Konzen, a talented 23 year old who was Microsoft's main systems programmer on the Macintosh. I knew Neil from his days as an early Apple II hobbyist, when we collaborated on adding features to an assembly language development system when he was only 16.

Jeff asked me what I was working on, and I told him about Thunderscan, which he seemed to be interested in. But when I mentioned that I was about to start some experiments with an application switching utility, his jaw dropped, and he looked like he couldn't believe what I said.

"That's just what we wanted to talk with you about!", he exclaimed, "It's great that you're already working on it".

Jeff explained that Microsoft had put a lot of effort into getting their applications to run well in the tiny space available in the 128K Macintosh, which they considered to be a key competitive advantage. But as things stood, the 512K Mac would undermine their efforts, since it allowed applications to be much larger. Plus, Lotus had recently announced an integrated application suite for the 512K Macintosh called Jazz that made it easy to quickly switch between different functional areas. But if the Macintosh could run multiple applications simultaneously, the small memory footprint of the Microsoft apps would continue to be advantageous, since their lower memory requirements meant that more of them could run concurrently, and users could put together customized application suites on their own. The purpose of the visit was to convince me to write an applications switcher under contract to Microsoft.

Neil Konzen had contemplated a potential design, which he conveyed to me in front of a whiteboard. He decided to use the single heap approach that I had rejected, along with a few interesting twists to minimize memory fragmentation. I told him about the alternate approach of using separate heapzones, and how I thought that it was probably worth it to trade some memory fragmentation for greater robustness. I told him that I would give his approach some more thought.

Finally, my afternoon at Microsoft culminated in a private meeting with their CEO, Bill Gates. Jeff ushered me into Bill's office and reviewed the afternoon's discussions for him, before excusing himself to leave us alone to negotiate a development deal. I had met Bill a few times during the course of Macintosh development, and while I respected his technical acumen, I was wary of his burgeoning reputation as a conniving businessman.

After exchanging a few pleasantries, and telling me how much the Macintosh mattered to Microsoft, he looked me in the eye and said, "You're a really good programmer, right? I think you must be a really good programmer."

"I guess so," I responded, not understanding why he was attempting to flatter me.

"Well, I think you are. How long do you think it will take to do this project? A month or two? I think a really good programmer like you could get it done in less than two months."

"I really have no idea," I replied, "I'm not far enough along to know if it's even feasible yet."

"Well, let's figure it out," he said in a slightly condescending tone. "I don't think it could be more than 10,000 lines of code, and a really good programmer like you should be able to write at least a thousand lines of code per week, so I think it will take you less than 10 weeks to write it, if you're as good as I think you are."

I didn't know how to respond, so I kept quiet and let him continue.

"And how much do you think a really good programmer should get paid? Around here we pay our best programmers around two thousand dollars per week. Do you think you should be paid more than that?"

"I don't know," I replied. I was finally beginning to see where he was coming from. Bill was trying to get me to brag that I could write the application switcher really quickly, so he could justify paying me a lower price for it.

"Well, I don't think that you could expect to get more than four thousand dollars per week, tops. Actually, I think that's too much, but let's go with that. If it takes ten weeks, and you get paid four thousand dollars per week, that means you should get paid $40,000 for writing it."

$40,000 didn't sound like very much to me, especially if it was as strategic to Microsoft as it seemed to be. I think Bill was expecting me to make a counteroffer, but I wasn't very enthusiastic about selling it to Microsoft regardless of compensation, since it really should eventually be part of the Mac OS.

"Listen, I really want to write this, completely independently from you guys, so you won't have to pay me anything to do it. I certainly don't want to negotiate a deal until I see how it turns out; there might be a show-stopper and I won't be able to get it to work at all. And if I pull it off, it really should be bundled with every 512K Macintosh."

Bill shifted his tactics. "OK, I don't really care if Microsoft owns it as long as it's available to our users. I want you to commit that you'll apply your best efforts to making sure that it runs well with our applications, and that you'll call Jeff if you run into any snags. We can talk again about publishing it later if you want to after you're further along. How does that sound?"

I told him that sounded good, and I promised to do my best to make it work great with Microsoft's applications, which I wanted to do anyway, since the Microsoft apps were important to most users. We shook hands and I departed on a positive note.

By the time I returned to my house in Palo Alto that evening, I was burning with the desire to see if I could get something going quickly. Even though still I had a few more days of work to complete the Thunderscan alpha release, I decided to see if I could write a proof of concept prototype of the application switcher first.

I would eventually have to write a user interface for selecting applications, but the proof of concept didn't have to worry about that; it was hardwired to run MacPaint, MacWrite, MacDraw and the Finder. I worked for 20 hours straight writing the core of the program, which worked by patching traps to extend a few essential system calls, like GetNextEvent, Launch and ExitToShell. The hardest part was going through all of the low memory locations, determining what needed to be swapped. It was incredibly satisfying to see it begin to work, crashing all the time at first, but gradually stabilizing as I tracked down various problems.

I had it working for an hour or so when I saw Bud Tribble return home. Bud had finally finished his M.D./Ph.D. program at the University of Washington, including interning for a year, but he decided that working on the Macintosh was more fun than being a doctor, so he had returned to Apple in his old job as software manager a few months earlier, in July 1984. Bud was living at Burrell Smith's house, which was next door to mine.

I dragged Bud over to my house to show him how I could rapidly switch between MacPaint, MacWrite and MacDraw. He was impressed, but to my surprise he complained that the switching, which was almost instantaneous, was actually too fast.

"I think it might be confusing to switch from one application to another without any feedback," he told me. "What if someone switches accidentally? Maybe you could use animation to make a smoother transition."

That sounded like a great idea to me. We decided that one application should scroll off the screen horizontally while another was scrolling on, which gave the users a simple, concrete mental model of the applications wrapped around a sort of Lazy Susan, which they could rotate to move the desired application to the visible area. I quickly wrote some fast scrolling routines, and was blown away by how cool it looked to see the applications zip across the screen.

I started showing my proof of concept demo to my friends at Apple, as well as a few user group demos, and it was very positively received. Unfortunately, I still had to finish up the product release of Thunderscan, which I barely managed to do by the end of November as I had promised. After taking a short vacation, I got back to work on what I was now calling "Switcher" in early December and by Christmas I had much of it implemented, including a simple UI for selecting applications and "Switcher Documents" for remembering sets of related applications.

In early January 1985, I got a phone call from Guy Kawasaki, one of Apple's third party evangelists, who told me that Apple was interested in buying Switcher, and that he was assigned to make that happen. The first step was arranging a demo for Steve Jobs.

I entered Steve's office with a bit of trepidation, because I thought that Switcher was worth at least a quarter of a million dollars to Apple, but I was sure that Steve would never want to pay me that much. But I was also proud of Switcher, and was interested in seeing how Steve would react to it.

I booted up my by now standard demo of MacWrite, MacPaint, MacDraw and the Finder, as well as a little maze generating program written by Steve Capps. I configured Switcher with the scrolling animation initially turned off, so it would have more impact when I showed it later. I demoed cutting and pasting between MacWrite, MacPaint and MacDraw, in seconds instead of minutes, and then I turned on the scrolling animation, and starting switching rapidly between them, in both directions.

"OK, I've seen enough, " Steve interrupted me. "It's great. Apple is going to bundle it with the Mac. Congratulations."

But then he paused, and stared at me for a moment with an incredibly intense gaze, as if he was sizing me up or maybe just trying to scare me.

"But I don't want you taking advantage of this situation. I'm not going to allow you to take advantage of Apple."

"What do you mean?" I asked him, genuinely puzzled.

"There's no way that you could have written that program without confidential information that you learned by working at Apple. You don't have the right to charge whatever you like for it."

I started to get angry. "The program is only half finished, and if I don't think you're paying me fairly, I won't be motivated to finish it."

Steve gave me another intense stare as he paused for a few seconds. Then he stated a single number, without explanation.

"One hundred thousand dollars."

"I don't know," I told him, "I think it's probably worth a lot more than that."

"Don't argue with me. $100,000 is fair, and you know it."

I didn't seem to have any alternative but to capitulate to Steve's price setting, since he's difficult to argue with and I really wanted Switcher bundled with the Mac. I eventually negotiated the final agreement with Guy Kawasaki, where, in addition to the $100,000, I managed to get a 10% royalty of the wholesale price if Apple sold Switcher separately, which Steve swore they would never do, but eventually the royalty delivered another $50,000.

Getting Switcher going wasn't that hard, but it was a very difficult program to finish, because it overturned some of the underlying assumptions that applications were making, yet it was committed to keeping everything working anyway. Much of the work in the latter stages involved testing it with every application that I could get my hands on and debugging crashes. Usually I could concoct some kind of technique that would mitigate the problem without causing worse problems elsewhere.

Predictably, the hardest part of finishing Switcher was making it work smoothly with the Microsoft applications. That was partially because Microsoft was a very early developer, and took liberties with the system that most developers would shy away from, but it was mostly because the instructions comprising their applications were encoded in pseudo-code to save space, in the tradition of the byte-code interpreters from Xerox, which Charles Simonyi advocated.

Unfortunately, the pseudo-code kept me from disassembling the program when it crashed, which made it more difficult to debug. I finally developed a debugging technique by single stepping through their interpreter, six instructions at a time to get to the instructions that were doing the work, but it was pretty painful. I was determined to slog through it because of the promise that I made when I visited Microsoft.

One of the last problems that I addressed before finishing the first release of Switcher in March 1985 had to do with applications hanging. If you're running multiple applications, you don't want one application hanging to take down all of them. I added a feature that allowed the user to kill the current application if it was hung up, by monitoring for a specific key combination during the vertical blanking interrupt handler.

I knew that I had to pick a very rare key combination, because you didn't want users killing their applications accidentally. I decided on shift-command-option-period, four keys held down at once, which I thought would be pretty hard to stumble into accidentally. But I was surprised when I got a call from Jeff Harbers at Microsoft.

"Hey, I like that abort feature that you just added, but you're going to have to change the key combination, because we're using that in Microsoft Word.", Jeff told me. Microsoft Word was very complex, and it possessed an enormous range of keyboard shortcuts, way too many, as far as I was concerned.

"OK, suggest something for me to change it to and I'll consider it," I told Jeff.

Jeff didn't have anything specific in mind, so he told me that he would get back to me soon. I had to laugh when he called me back the next day, and told me that he wanted to withdraw his request and that I should keep shift-command-option-period as the abort sequence.

"OK, that sounds good to me, " I told him. "But why the change? Doesn't it still conflict with Word?"

"We'll change Word in the next release not to use it. The problem was that we couldn't find a safe sequence - I guess we're already using every key combination!"

I officially released the finished version of Switcher in April 1985, and I maintained it for a few versions after that. Eventually, I handed it off to Phil Goldman, a tremendous young programmer from Princeton who was recently hired at Apple, who went on to write MultiFinder (with Erich Ringewald), Switcher's eventual successor, in 1987.

item.title: Brave Search API now accepts agentic payments via the x402 protocol (183 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://brave.com/blog/search-api-agentic-payments/, See on Hacker News

Blog Brave Search news

The Brave Search API, our developer tool for building applications with data from the Web, is adding support for instant, pay-as-you-go, agentic payments enabled by the open x402 payment protocol. Developers and autonomous AI agents that specifically require agentic search can now programmatically query Brave’s independent search index, ground agent responses, and settle requests in real time, which eliminates the need for traditional API key management.

Integrating x402 with the Brave Search API makes it easier for an agentic harness to leverage Brave Search API via a CLI wallet, as Brave runs its own facilitator accepting USDC on the Base blockchain, with acceptance on other networks and with other stablecoins incoming soon. This allows a Brave Search API user the ability to pay for LLM Context (agentic grounding) or general web search on-demand, without first creating an account and selecting a plan. Instead, simply transfer USDC stablecoin to your agent’s wallet via the Base network and it’s ready to access the same high-quality search results powered by Brave’s search engine.

How does it work?

Brave Search API endpoints behind x402 require payment on every request rather than authentication. A request sent without payment receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response that states the price of that search and the payment details needed to pay it. The agent signs a USDC payment for that amount and retries the request with the signed payment attached. Once the payment is verified, the search runs and results are returned with a receipt of the transaction that occurred on the Base blockchain.

Get started today

Pricing follows Brave’s published API rates: LLM Context, an API designed specifically for providing search context for agents, will cost $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Additionally, web (search for humans), news, image, video, and local endpoints will also be available for $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Gas fees for transacting on the Base blockchain will be covered for a limited time. Since each request carries its own payment, a Brave Search API account is no longer needed to use the service.

The easiest path to query via x402 is to install Purl Wallet, a Stripe-developed CLI wallet for your agent. Set up your wallet, top it off using Base-native USDC, and start querying today.

Ready to build pay-as-you-go search into your apps or AI agents? Check out our Brave Search x402 Proxy Documentation and explore: https://api-dashboard.search.brave.com/documentation/guides/agent-payments

item.title: Nvidia employees petition to bring back Jensen Huang (720 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.wired.com/story/nvidia-employees-petition-for-jensen-huangs-return/, See on Hacker News

Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.

An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.

“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.

“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.

One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”

The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment.

Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email.

Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.

It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.

One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED.

Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.”

Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

item.title: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer (295 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://edge0.ai/blog/introducing-edge0-145b-frontier-ai-capabilities-on-your-own-computer, See on Hacker News

Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer.

On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity.

This release addresses those constraints in four ways:

The constraint What Edge0-145B makes possible
Large models are difficult to run on personal hardware. A 145B model runs locally on a compatible laptop, with reported peak memory of 29GB and decoding above 80 tokens/s.
Small on-device models can fall short on demanding tasks. Coding, reasoning, and instruction-following results are competitive with specific frontier cloud models, as the comparisons below show.
A useful assistant needs to finish work, not just answer questions. The model plans, writes and runs code, debugs errors, and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs, and PCB designs.
Cloud workflows bring recurring fees, sensitive-data restrictions, and network dependence. Local inference incurs no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees; data can stay on the computer, and core capabilities keep working offline. Hardware and electricity still cost money.

We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products.

Get the model weights, explore the inference framework, or try the Edge0 App.

How We Make 100B+ Parameter AI Run on a Personal Computer

Edge0-145B Laptop Performance: Memory, Speed, and Power

Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks.

Requirement Reported Edge0-145B result What it enables
Memory 29GB peak memory Runs on a compatible personal laptop, such as a MacBook Pro, without a server.
Prompt processing 1,100+ tokens/s prefill Processes long prompts, including dozens of pages of code, before generation begins.
Generation 80+ tokens/s decode Generates faster than a person reads.
Power Approximately 120W typical power Sustains operation without throttling in the reported setup.
Long tasks 128K–256K context Maintains essentially the same speed on long inputs, supporting extended work.

Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware.

On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards.

Why On-Device Models Have Stayed Small

Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026. Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, while Google's Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions. Even a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB of memory.

Larger models faced a memory wall. Model weights occupy storage and must be read during generation, competing for limited memory and bandwidth with the operating system and other apps. Even an aggressively compressed 35B model could need approximately 20GB of memory, far more than a phone could make available.

Compute, bandwidth, and power created competing constraints. Larger models offered more capability, but strained memory capacity, generation speed, and battery life. Making models smaller helped them fit, often at the cost of capability.

Privacy alone could not close that gap. Apple Intelligence protected user data, but Apple acknowledged that its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge. The prevailing assumption was that on-device intelligence could not match the cloud.

Under the Hood of Edge0: Four Layers of Model and Inference Design

We designed Edge0-145B and its inference engine together to reduce the memory and data movement that make large models difficult to run locally. The design spans architecture, training, loading, and scheduling.

Architecture: share large matrices across sparse experts. Sharing matrices substantially reduces the weights that must be stored and moved while keeping the expert count unchanged. Each group of 64 experts shares two large matrices, while each expert retains a small set of parameters that captures its differences. Previously, every expert stored a complete set of matrices. Of the model's 145B total parameters, only approximately 10B participate in computation on each inference step.

Training: build for local execution from day one. We train the model in its on-device architecture from the outset, with deployment constraints built into its design. This avoids treating local deployment as a compression or pruning step after training a cloud model.

Loading: pipeline GPU memory, system memory, and SSD access. Reading and computation overlap across three storage tiers, avoiding serial waits. Frequently used “hot experts” remain in GPU memory. An expert library of approximately 40GB sits in system memory, with experts brought into GPU memory as needed. Approximately 48GB of vocabulary data resides on the SSD and is read on demand.

Scheduling: use the CPU and GPU together. The GPU computes cached experts while the CPU handles the remaining work in parallel. Speculative decoding verifies multiple candidate tokens at once, spreading the cost of reading weights across more output tokens. These choices support the reported 80+ tokens/s decode rate.

Model and inference-engine design work together to make 100B+ parameter inference practical on personal computers. Source: internal testing.

Together, these changes let parameter counts grow from tens of billions to more than a hundred billion without proportional increases in memory use, power consumption, and latency.

What Edge0 Can Do: Anything From Chat to Complex Work on Your Computer

Edge0-145B can carry a complex task through to a usable result. Its coding and reasoning capabilities support local workflows that combine planning, tool use, execution, debugging, and visual checks. The benchmarks establish its capabilities; the demonstrations show how it puts them to work.

Coding and reasoning that rival frontier cloud models

Edge0-145B is competitive with specific frontier cloud models across coding, reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following:

  • Coding: It scores 64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1, ahead of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 58.7 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 54.4.
  • Reasoning and knowledge: It scores 90.4 on GPQA-Diamond, close to DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 90.8 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 91.3.
  • Instruction following: It scores 80.6 on IFBench, ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 79.2 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 62.5.

Its 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 also exceeds Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 83.3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731's 82.7, and Claude's 78.2. On AA-LCR, Edge0-145B scores 79.3 to Claude's 78.0. These comparisons apply to the named models and evaluations.

Edge0, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Claude results come from Edge0's internal evaluations. Claude-Opus-4.6 has no public DeepSWE 1.1 score. For Flint, Muse Glimmer, and Gemma 4, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and IFBench results come from the Recursive Flint evaluation; HLE, GPQA, and AA-LCR results come from Artificial Analysis.

The largest gains over Qwen3.8-27B, a mainstream on-device model baseline, are in agent and coding work: 18.5% on Terminal-Bench and 53.1% on DeepSWE. The relative gains on HLE, GPQA, and IFBench are 14.9%, 1.3%, and 1.4%, respectively.

DeepSWE 1.1 and Terminal-Bench 2.1 evaluate agent and coding work. HLE, GPQA-Diamond, and IFBench cover reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following. The complete evaluation setup, hardware environment, and reproduction instructions are being released with our technical report.

Competitive capability with a smaller memory footprint

Edge0-145B combines a 72.8 mean score across six benchmarks with 29GB measured peak memory. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next averages 71.7, with an estimated 70GB footprint for standard 4-bit deployment. That puts Edge0-145B at about 40% of the estimated baseline memory while delivering comparable or higher capability, enabling local use on a 48GB laptop.

Edge0-145B 72.8 29GB
Edge0-120B 68.9 29GB
Qwen3.8-27B 66.1 Approximately 18GB*
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 71.7 Approximately 70GB*
DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 70.1 Approximately 87GB*

The means cover DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, HLE, GPQA-Diamond, IFBench, and AA-LCR. Edge0 memory figures are measured internal peaks. Asterisked baseline figures are estimates for standard 4-bit deployment and remain to be measured. Claude is excluded because it is cloud-only and has no DeepSWE score.

[Figure: Quality versus peak memory, with 48GB laptop and 64GB workstation capacities marked. Lower memory and higher scores are better; the chart's vertical axis does not start at zero.]

Local agents that plan, code, run, and check their work

A single natural-language request can start an entire local workflow. Edge0-145B breaks down the requirements, plans the steps, writes code, and calls tools to run it. When something fails, it debugs and repairs the code. It then takes screenshots to inspect the result and keeps iterating until the work is complete.

These projects often take dozens of rounds of planning, execution, and review. Local inference means those additional conversations, code revisions, and visual analyses incur no corresponding cloud-model token or API charges. Code and data can stay on the computer, and core model capabilities work offline.

Video production: generating Tesla's Roadster explainer within an hour

Edge0-145B produced an explainer about how Roadster could fly, handling technical research, scriptwriting, asset generation, and editing. We asked it to make the principles understandable to a general audience. The model ran locally without cloud-model calls or cloud token consumption, avoiding network round trips for inference.

The video was generated within an hour. Producing comparable work manually would have taken a director and scriptwriter, a 3D modeler, an editor, and a physics expert a month. An AI video workflow could previously cost more than hundreds of dollars; local inference eliminates the corresponding cloud-model token and API fees.

3D modeling: a Manhattan city scene in Blender

Edge0-145B built a 3D scene of Manhattan within an hour. Working in Blender from text and reference images, it constructed the scene, adjusted materials and lighting, and iterated on the rendered output.

The workflow brings visual inspection, code generation, and revision together inside Blender. The model works with objects, spatial relationships, and the creative goal, going beyond the pixels in a reference image. It inspects the result, writes code, and makes changes without handing those steps back to a person. The entire process stays local.

Creating a Manhattan-scale city scene manually would typically cost approximately $12,000-18,000 and take at least a month. A leading cloud model would still incur more than $150 in cloud token charges. Edge0-145B completes the local inference without those cloud-model token fees.

Game development: playable games and a medieval city

Edge0-145B can create playable games locally. We also used its 3D modeling capabilities to build an original medieval capital for a fantasy RPG and render a 20-second fly-through at game-trailer quality.

The model planned the city independently and built it from scratch in Blender: city walls, more than a thousand old-town homes, a plaza fountain, a Gothic twin-tower facade, a rib-vaulted nave, and stained-glass windows.

The fixed camera path made errors visible. Geometry clipping, occlusion, or incorrect proportions would appear along the route, so the model inspected the renders and corrected its work as it built. The workflow ran entirely locally.

A leading cloud model required hundreds of tool calls and hundreds of millions of tokens for a single completion, using the same prompt, reference images, and camera route. Edge0-145B delivered it on a laptop without cloud-model token or API fees for local inference. An art team would typically spend weeks and thousands of dollars producing a city scene to this standard.

Hardware control: code that flies a real drone

Edge0-145B wrote the program for a real drone from one instruction: “Write a drone program that navigates through obstacles and finds a red backpack.”

It generated the flight-control and visual-recognition programs locally. The drone then took off indoors, navigated through a dense row of obstacle poles, searched autonomously, and located the red backpack beside a wall. The task required no human-written code and no cloud call.

Hardware developers can describe the behavior they want and have the model turn it into a program for a real device, without moving repeatedly between an editor, documentation, and debugging tools.

PCB design: from KiCad layout to an assembly animation

Edge0-145B took a PCB design from component placement through an assembly visualization. We asked it to design a board for itself. It started from scratch in KiCad, placed components, routed a two-layer board, and imported the design into Unreal Engine 5. It then set up cameras and lighting and rendered an animation of PCB fabrication and assembly.

A single computer delivered work that previously required a hardware engineer and a 3D designer to hand tasks back and forth over several days. Schematics and board layouts can stay on the team's own hardware, supporting trade-secret protection and data-handling requirements without uploading the designs to a cloud model.

Why Edge0: A Full Stack for On-Device AI

Useful on-device AI requires model development, inference engineering, and hardware adaptation to work together. Our progress rests on three capabilities: developing complementary models quickly, optimizing the full stack, and carrying lessons from each deployment into the next.

Our September release of Edge0-35B showed what that approach could deliver on a phone. Its launch post passed 1.2 million views on its first day without paid promotion in overseas communities. Researchers and technical experts at OpenAI, NVIDIA, Qualcomm, and other companies shared it, and the model reached No. 1 on Hugging Face's overall Trending chart.

We released the model weights and unified inference framework together, giving companies and researchers a standard approach they could reproduce. The release helped move the discussion of on-device AI from a few billion parameters to the 35B tier.

Four Model Families for On-Device AI

Over the past year, we released 200 models across four families. Each handles a different part of the work, from listening and speaking to fast decisions, memory, and complex agent tasks.

Model family Role Models and capabilities
Edge0 Complex agent tasks and vibe coding 145B and 120B models for laptops; 35B and 8B models for phones. The laptop models support vibe coding, while the phone models support agent tasks.
Audio8 Listening and speaking ASR-Infinite and 3B, 0.6B, and 0.1B ASR models for speech recognition; 0.6B and 0.1B TTS models for speech synthesis; and a 0.1B Chat model for end-to-end voice interaction.
Decision0 Fast decisions 0.6B and 3B models covering text, speech, and vision, with multimodal decisions in approximately 40 milliseconds.
Embedding0 Memory A 0.6B multimodal embedding model for text, speech, images, video, and files, supporting local long-term memory and retrieval-augmented generation \(RAG\).

The portfolio spans tens of millions to more than a hundred billion parameters. Both Edge0 and Audio8 have reached No. 1 on Hugging Face's Trending chart.

Models and Inference Systems Designed Together

We develop the model and the inference framework together, building hardware constraints into training and optimizing the engine for different chips. This connects model capability with the software and hardware needed to use it locally.

That work requires expertise in model development, inference frameworks, and low-level hardware adaptation. The combination is difficult for a company focused only on model development to reproduce.

Hardware Optimizations That Carry into Each Deployment

Each deployment gives us reusable optimizations for the next chip, model, or product. This matters because on-device hardware is fragmented: NPU architectures differ, as does support for numerical formats such as INT4, INT8, and FP4. A general-purpose model cannot automatically make full use of every chip.

We adapt to individual platforms. Our portfolio now covers 95% of mainstream chip platforms, including Qualcomm, BES, Rockchip, Allwinner, D-Robotics, and NVIDIA, across headphones, glasses, phones, PCs, and robots. This is portfolio-wide coverage; model requirements vary, and it does not mean every device can run Edge0-145B.

That deployment work now spans more than 5 million production devices. Our open-source models passed 15 million downloads within three months. By October 2026, we had more than 110,000 customer organizations.

The portfolio figures come from company papers and internal testing. They describe the broader Edge0 portfolio; the 145B performance results in this article apply specifically to Edge0-145B.

For Edge0-145B, day-one support covers macOS, Windows, and Linux, including Apple M-series chips and NVIDIA platforms such as RTX Spark, RTX 4090, and RTX 5090. The release includes one-click deployment tools and hardware guides.

The Future of On-Device AI and the Cloud

More complex work can stay on the device as local models approach cloud-level capability. Privacy, cost control, and offline access have long favored local execution; the remaining question was whether an on-device model could do the work. Edge0-145B expands the range of tasks for which it can.

Why More AI Work Can Stay Local

Local execution addresses four practical obstacles to adopting cloud-only AI:

  • Control cloud-model costs. Local inference adds no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees as usage grows.
  • Keep sensitive data local. Code, documents, and business records can stay on the hardware, giving teams control over data handling.
  • Sustain a responsive experience. Model and inference-engine design address response speed, power use, system responsiveness, and continuous operation together.
  • Keep core capabilities available offline. Local tasks continue when connectivity drops; features that depend on online information or services still need a connection.

From Cloud First to More Complex Work On-Device

We see the division of work between devices and the cloud shifting through three stages.

Before September 2026: cloud first, with on-device support. Apple Intelligence reflected this stage: it protected privacy, but handled a limited range of tasks locally while more demanding work relied on cloud capabilities.

After Edge0-35B's September 10 release: everyday tasks locally, complex tasks in the cloud. Local models could take on frequent requests that needed immediate responses. For one leading headphone manufacturer, our hybrid solution now handles 92% of AI usage on-device and 8% in the cloud. Everyday conversation accounts for most use cases on consumer wearables.

With Edge0-145B: toward on-device first, with cloud support. Vibe coding and other complex tasks can now run on a personal computer, giving teams more scope to choose local execution. This extends the range of work that can stay on the device while preserving the cloud for tasks and hardware that need it.

The diagram shows the shift from cloud-first AI to everyday local tasks and then more complex local work. Its colored areas are schematic, not measured usage shares.

Where Cloud AI Still Fits

Hardware constraints still determine which model fits. Compute capacity, heat, and battery life matter: Edge0-35B runs on phones, while Edge0-145B runs on suitably equipped laptops. A very low-compute device cannot currently run a 145B model locally. It needs a smaller model suited to its hardware or cloud access to a model of that size.

Cross-device long-term memory and searches requiring highly current information still require cloud services. Local and cloud models can work together; the appropriate split depends on the task, the hardware, and the information it needs.

The aim is to make local execution a practical choice for demanding work, with a capable model that can keep working close to the person using it. That is the next step toward our goal of enabling intelligence at zero distance for everybody.

Get Started with Edge0

Download the models to run locally, evaluate or fine-tune them, and build them into your own products:

  • Model weights: Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B on Hugging Face.
  • Inference framework and deployment guides: Edge0 on GitHub.
  • Try it without environment setup: Download the Edge0 App. Its core model capabilities work offline, without an account or usage quota.
  • Community: Join us on Discord.

For hardware or product integrations, reach the Edge0 team through GitHub or contact@autoark.ai.

Cite this report

Executive Summary

Our forensic analysis of publicly released AI models finds evidence that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models. Six models released by these companies since April 2026 contain numerical patterns matching Blackwell hardware, whereas earlier models from the same companies match NVIDIA’s older Hopper generation. The findings suggest that several leading Chinese AI developers have begun using Blackwell to train their newest models. U.S. officials and press reports had already alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, without publishing technical evidence.

The evidence comes entirely from the models’ own published weights, rather than from leaks or insider accounts. We recover traces of the models’ initial values, and then search for the hardware configurations and initial configurations that reproduce them; for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, we also confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips. The fingerprint identifies how the weights were created and supports, without proving, the inference that Blackwell also performed the training. Specially configured AMD hardware, which is also restricted from export to China, is the only alternative we have identified; we have excluded it for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and consider it very unlikely for the other five models. Notably, our findings provide technical evidence of access to advanced computing hardware, but do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated.

Main Findings

  1. Six models from four Chinese labs read as Blackwell-trained. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match NVIDIA’s Blackwell-class B200 or B300 chips, which have 148 processor cores (called streaming multiprocessors, or SMs). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro and Ling-3.1-flash match the GB200 or GB300 chips, also Blackwell-class, which have 152 processor cores. Kimi K3.1-Pro starts from the same seed as K3, and may be a checkpoint of K3 with further post-training.
  2. Chinese labs started training on Blackwell relatively recently. DeepSeek’s models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3 (released in December 2024), and as Blackwell from DeepSeek V4 (released in April 2026). Moonshot’s models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 (January 2026) and as Blackwell from K3 (July 2026). One Moonshot model sits in between: Kimi K2.7-Code, posted six weeks before K3, is built on the Hopper-era weights but contains a small part that matches the B200 or B300. MiniMax’s models read as Hopper through M2.7 (April 2026) and as Blackwell from M3 (June 2026). Ant Group’s Ling-3.0-flash (August 2026) reads as Hopper, while its Ling-3.1-flash (October 2026) reads as Blackwell. The Hopper readings do not identify a specific chip: H800s, H100 SXMs and H200s share the same fingerprint.
  3. Not every Chinese AI lab has switched to Blackwell. The newest models we could read from Alibaba (Qwen), Zhipu (GLM), Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan says its LongCat-2.0 was trained entirely on “AI ASIC superpods,” and we found no NVIDIA fingerprint in the model weights it’s released.
  4. The method gets known answers right. For 24 specific models, the developer has publicly said what hardware was used. In every case, our method agrees with the public announcement. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of its training, reads as 152 SMs, the same as Kimi K3.
  5. The matches are far stronger than chance would explain. Even unrelated numbers can appear to match when enough combinations are tried. Across the roughly 6 trillion seed-and-layout combinations in our search, the strongest chance match would be expected to reach about 8 sigma—a measure of how far a result stands above ordinary random variation. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma. Even the weakest individual test we report reaches 20 sigma.
  6. The training runs were data-center scale. From each model’s size and the amount of data it was trained on, we estimate that each run needed roughly 500 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs for two to three months (Table 2), assuming each model was trained on the hardware that initialized it. The same arithmetic applied to DeepSeek-V3 gives 2,000 to 2,500 chips; DeepSeek disclosed 2,048. At roughly $70,000 per GPU—the cost implied by a Wall Street Journal report that about 36,000 Blackwell chips being installed in Malaysia for ByteDance’s use would cost more than $2.5 billion—the largest of these clusters would cost $150 million to $200 million, and the five together more than half a billion dollars. These figures cover only the final training runs; the labs’ total spending on export-controlled GPUs is likely in the billions of dollars.
