item.title: Show HN: My $300 embroidery machine needed a subscription, so I built my own app (491 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/simpsoka/zigzag, See on Hacker News

Visit zigzag.diy

ZigZag is a visual embroidery editor built in Rust for performance, with built-in MCP (Model Context Protocol) support so AI agents can create and edit designs alongside you. Turn SVG artwork into stitches, fine-tune it in the editor, and export PES, DST, EXP, JEF, or VP3 for broad compatibility with embroidery machines—or send designs directly to a Brother Skitch (PP1) over Bluetooth.

Draw in Illustrator, draw in ZigZag, or let an agent draw. The Rust engine and zigzag command-line tool power the same workflow outside the editor.

See ZigZag in action

zigzag-demo.mp4

Download for Mac

Download ZigZag.dmg

For Apple Silicon and Intel Macs, macOS 11 or later. Open the DMG, then drag ZigZag into Applications. The release is signed and notarized by Apple. No Rust installation is needed.

Download for Windows

Download ZigZag for Windows — the ZigZag-<version>-x86_64-windows.zip asset on the latest release.

For 64-bit Windows 10 (version 1709 or later) and Windows 11. Unzip it and double-click ZigZag.exe. Windows SmartScreen warns on apps without a Microsoft-trusted signature the first time they run; click More info → Run anyway. No Rust installation is needed.

Release notes and checksums · Publishing a release

zigzag/
  src/svg.rs              SVG import (usvg): fill and stroke parts, transforms, text
  src/document/           editable document; settings saved back into SVG ids,
                          layout edits as SVG transforms, lettering
  src/params.rs           stitch settings tokens + fabric presets
  src/stitch/fill.rs      tatami fill (scanline sections, staggered rows)
  src/stitch/satin.rs     satin columns: two rails, auto-satin, underlays, short stitches
  src/stitch/stroke.rs    running / triple-run stitch
  src/boolean.rs          polygon booleans and offsets (i_overlay)
  src/design.rs           planner: overlap removal, cap order, routing, trims
  src/checks.rs           digitizing checks (sizes, widths, lettering, hoop)
  src/formats/            PES (+PEC), DST, EXP, JEF, VP3, Skitch PEN writers;
                          PES/PEC/DST/EXP/JEF readers; preview; worksheet
  src/machine/            Skitch Bluetooth protocol (+ btleplug client, `ble` feature)
  src/studio/             editor (egui on OpenGL via glow) + MCP server (`gui` feature)
  src/mcp_bridge.rs       stdio ↔ HTTP bridge for MCP clients that launch a command

Build

cargo build --release                        # CLI + MCP bridge, no system deps
cargo build --release --features gui,ble     # + the studio editor and Skitch upload

Linux needs the usual X11/Wayland and OpenGL dev libraries for gui. libdbus is vendored for ble.

Stitch types

Type What it does Works on
Fill (tatami) Staggered rows, any angle, with underlay (edge walk + rows) and pull compensation Filled shapes
Satin Zigzag column between two rails, with center/contour/zigzag underlay, pull compensation and short stitches on tight curves; plain, S-stitch or zig-zag top stitching; several threads across the column (multicolor satin) Strokes (any width); Ink/Stitch-style two-rail paths with rungs; filled shapes: rings use inner/outer outline, bars/letters/crescents split at their tips (auto-satin), or border follows the outline
Run Running stitch, single or triple (bean) Strokes and outlines
Contour Rows that follow the outline inward, or one spiral out from the center (Ink/Stitch's circular fill) Filled shapes
Blanket E-stitch: a line with prongs into the shape Edges, appliqué
Appliqué Placement line → stop → tack-down → stop → satin cover Filled shapes
Manual Every path point is a needle point Imported machine files, pen tool
Meander One wandering line through the shape, quilting style: light and soft Filled shapes
Ripple Open running-stitch rows following the outline, or one spiral Filled shapes
Cross-stitch A grid of X's, sewn as rows of half-crosses out and back Filled shapes
Tartan Woven stripes in several threads (a mirrored sett you edit in the panel), each thread its own color block Filled shapes

Satins wider than 7 mm are auto-split (shorter, staggered stitches) and use auto spacing (narrow columns more open, wide ones denser).

Planner features:

  • Remove overlaps: fill hidden under later objects isn't sewn (keeps 0.5 mm of overlap).
  • Cap order: center-out, bottom-up, grouped by color, still respecting layering.
  • Routing: travel stitches stay inside shapes: straight across where a straight line stays inside, otherwise round the inside of the outline (Ink/Stitch's underpath), so a fill with a cut-out is sewn with few or no cuts. Trims only where neither works (up to 50 mm of travel).
  • Sewing control per object: a start and an end point (where the thread comes in and leaves, so the next object is close), trim after, stop after (to lay foam or trim appliqué). The document can also connect objects up to N mm apart with running stitches instead of cuts.
  • Fabric presets: standard, thin cotton cap, structured cap, knit.
  • Checks: narrow fills, wide/narrow satins, small lettering, tiny gaps, fully covered objects, hoop fit.
  • Group colors: reorder to cut thread changes without breaking layering.

Mac app

On a Mac with Rust and the Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install):

packaging/macos/make-app.sh --install    # builds ZigZag.app and copies it to /Applications
packaging/macos/make-app.sh --dmg        # also makes dist/ZigZag-<version>.dmg to share
packaging/macos/make-app.sh --universal  # one app for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs
packaging/macos/make-app.sh --release    # the DMG to publish: universal, signed, notarized

--release signs with your Developer ID and has Apple notarize the app and the DMG, so it opens on any Mac without warnings. Once, beforehand: add a Developer ID Application certificate (Xcode › Settings › Accounts › Manage Certificates › +), make an app-specific password at account.apple.com, and save the notarization credentials in your keychain:

xcrun notarytool store-credentials zigzag-notary --apple-id YOUR_APPLE_ID --team-id YOUR_TEAM_ID

The app bundles the studio, the zigzag command-line tool and the MCP bridge. To use the command line from anywhere: ln -s /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag /usr/local/bin/zigzag. For Claude Desktop, point the MCP config at /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag-mcp.

Without --release the app is signed ad hoc, not notarized. It opens normally on the Mac that built it. On another Mac, macOS blocks it the first time: open System Settings › Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway (on macOS 14 and earlier, right-click the app and choose Open instead). macOS asks for Bluetooth permission the first time you send to the Skitch.

Studio

The approved embroidered icons live in packaging/macos/AppIcon.png (light) and packaging/macos/AppIcon-dark.png (dark). The Mac build regenerates both multi-resolution .icns files; run bash packaging/macos/make-icons.sh to regenerate them separately. Finder and the unopened app use the light icon. While the studio is running, its Dock icon follows the app's light/dark theme, including the ZIGZAG_THEME=light|dark override.

zigzag-studio [design.svg|logo.png] [--mcp-port 7878 | --no-mcp | --mcp-stdio]

Laid out like Illustrator, styled like a Mac app:

  • Tools down the left edge: Select (V), Direct Selection (A), Hand (H), Pen (P): click for corners, drag for curves (Option breaks the handles, Shift keeps 45°, Space moves the point being placed); while drawing, Option lends it the Anchor Point tool (drag a segment to bend it, a handle to move it alone, click a smooth point for a corner) and ⌘ lends Direct Selection (drag a point or handle, then keep drawing), and on a selected path Option-drag bends a segment too. Illustrator's Pen group is behind it: Add Anchor Point (+) clicks a point onto an outline without changing its shape, Delete Anchor Point (-) clicks one out (Option swaps the two while held), and Anchor Point (Shift+C) converts points between smooth and corner and drags one handle alone. Press and hold the Pen (or right-click it) for the group's flyout, Option-click it to step through the group, or tear the group off into a toolbar of its own with the strip at the flyout's edge; the Shape tools work the same way. Brush (B), with VectorCraft's path clean-up tools in its group: Smooth (drag along a path to take the wobble out: fewer points, smoother curves; Smoothness in the bar above), Path Eraser (drag across a path to cut that part away) and Join (scrub between two open ends to join them, or an open path's two ends to close it). Shapes (M rectangle, L ellipse, \ line; hold or right-click for polygon and star), Fill Angle (G), Measure (I), Text (T). Below them, the selection's thread swatch: click it for the thread color picker.

  • Curves, the Illustrator way: the Pen clicks corners and click-drags curves (Option while dragging breaks the handle for a sharp turn; Shift keeps points and handles at 45°; hold Space to move the point you're placing). Click the last point to make it a corner, or drag from it to start the next curve in a new direction. Click the first point to close a shape; Enter, Esc, ⌘-click or another tool ends a line and keeps it. With a path selected, the Pen continues it from an open end, adds a point on its outline, deletes a point you click, and Option-click turns a point corner ↔ smooth (Option-drag pulls out new handles). While drawing, click another open path's end to join the two into one. The cursor shows what a click will do. Direct Selection drags points and handles of any shape from your SVG (circles and rects become paths); dragging a curve bends it under the pointer (Option-drag bends a straight one; a plain drag moves it); Delete removes points, arrows nudge them.

  • Smart guides while drawing (View › Smart Guides, ⌘U): Pen points, shape corners and dragged points land on other objects' anchors and centers, where two outlines cross, on an outline, on 45° rays from the last point (level and upright handles too), or in line with any of those, with a magenta label saying which ("anchor", "intersect", "path", "align"…). With Shift, a point keeps its 45° angle and slides into line with the nearest target.

  • Round corners: in Direct Selection a small circle sits inside each sharp corner; drag it in to round the corners (the selected points', or all of them), each only as far as its sides allow. Object › Path › Round Corners… does the same with a radius and Round, Inverted or Chamfer, previewed live.

  • Brush (B), after Illustrator's Paintbrush: paint a line freehand and it comes out smooth, sewn as a satin column at the width you set (or as a running stitch). Smoothness takes out the hand's wobble; sharp turns stay sharp; end where you began to close the line. The cursor is a circle as wide as the satin.

  • Shapes, the Illustrator way: Rectangle (M), Ellipse (L), Polygon, Star and Line (\). Drag from a corner; Option draws from the center, Shift makes a square or circle, keeps a polygon or star upright and a line at 45°. While dragging a polygon or star, ↑/↓ add or remove sides or points. Click without dragging to type an exact size. The bar at the top of the canvas switches shapes and sets corner radius, sides, points and the star's inner radius. Closed shapes come in as fills, lines as runs, in the current thread.

  • Path tools: Object › Pathfinder (Unite, Minus Front, Intersect, Exclude; also buttons in the Transform panel when two or more objects are selected) and Object › Path (Offset Path…, Outline Stroke, Simplify…, Round Corners…, Clean Up…). Simplify… is VectorCraft's slider, from fewest points to closest to the original, previewed live, with Auto-Simplify picking the level for the selection's size. Clean Up… removes stray points, objects too small to sew (under 1 mm by default) and extra points (points on top of each other, points in the middle of straight lines), showing how many of each it found first. Results come back as smooth curves with their real corners (least-squares curve fitting), not as many-sided polygons.

  • Logos from images (Image Trace): open, drop or place a PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP or TIFF and the Trace Image window traces it into flat-color shapes, previewed on your hat's color. Choose how many colors (or Auto), the width, detail and the smallest speck to keep; remove the white background; snap every color to your Brother, Janome or own palette's threads; and sew thin lines as single lines. Flat logos trace exactly (edges placed to a fraction of a pixel, corners restored, circles and straight lines exact); photos are posterized. The command line traces too: zigzag convert logo.png -o logo.pes.

  • Contextual task bar: under the selection, the next things you'd do: its stitch type, its thread, Edit Points, Round Corners, Simplify, Unite (two or more), Duplicate. View › Contextual Task Bar (or its ••• menu) hides it.

  • Ask an agent: the Agent panel (full height in the left dock; the sparkle at the bottom of the tool strip opens and closes it, and ⌘K or Window › Ask Agent… opens it with the prompt ready) runs Claude Code or Codex in the background, connected to this studio's MCP server, so you watch it build the design. It can only use the design tools (no shell, no file edits). The transcript shows what it said and each step, with a spinner on the one running (the one place it's shown; collapse the panel and its header shows the step and the time instead). On the canvas, the objects it's working on get a moving outline, a shimmer and a label saying what it's doing (Drawing, Placing, Restyling…), for any agent connected over MCP, not just the panel's. The panel is named for the agent (Claude Code or Codex; switch in its ≡ menu); + in its header starts a new chat, Stop ends a run. Uses the claude or codex command you've already signed in to. Like any panel it can float, join another as a tab or dock right; sharing a dock it sits at the bottom, under a divider you drag to give it more room.

  • Thread colors and palettes: the picker shows the nearest Brother/Janome thread, a palette to click (Brother, Janome or your own), and a small custom color field. Make palettes from scratch, from the design, or from a thread kit you own (the palette's ≡ menu › New Palette from Thread Kit: Brother's 12, 40 and 22 color sets, or 40 + 22 for all 61; then Match All keeps a design to the threads in your box), add the selection's thread with +, right-click to remove; they're remembered between launches.

  • Threads panel: the design's threads in sewing order (each color block numbered, with its stitches, and "stop" where the same thread comes twice running) or By Color (each thread once, with how many objects use it). Click a row to select what it sews; click a swatch to change that block's thread, or in By Color that thread everywhere. Group Colors and the count of color changes and trims are under the list. The panel's ≡ menu has Match All to the chosen palette, and Show Palette puts a palette to click under the list (off by default, since the thread picker has the same palettes).

  • Panels, the Illustrator way: the Agent has the left dock to itself; Objects, Stitch, Transform, Lettering, Threads and Document are on the right. The design's issues are in the status bar (bottom right): a warning sign with a count, or a check when all's well; click it (or Window › Issues) for the list, each linked to its object. Drag a panel by its header to reorder it, move it to the other dock, or drop it on the canvas to float it (each panel's ≡ menu also has Dock Left / Dock Right / Float). Drop a panel on another panel's header and they share it as tabs; drag a tab out (or use Separate in the ≡ menu) to part them, drag the header to move the group. » at the top of a dock collapses it to a strip of icons for a bigger canvas: click an icon and the panel flies out beside the strip (drag an icon to move that panel). Click a header to collapse a panel; Window › Reset Panels puts everything back. The layout is remembered.

  • Tabs, one per document (as in VectorCraft and Illustrator): Open, drop or New opens a file in a tab of its own over the canvas (the empty document you start with makes way for the first one); a file that's already open just comes forward. Each tab keeps its own undo history, selection, zoom and stitches. Click a tab to switch, ⌃Tab / ⌃⇧Tab (or Window › Next / Previous Document) to step through them, drag one to reorder, middle-click or its × (or File › Close, ⌘W) to close it; + opens a new document and » lists every tab when they don't all fit. A dot in place of the × marks unsaved changes, and closing such a tab asks whether to save it first. Right-click a tab for Close Other Tabs and Copy Path. Quitting doesn't ask: every tab comes back next time, each with its unsaved changes.

  • Menu bar (File, Edit, Object, View, Window) with the usual ⌘ shortcuts. It's the real macOS menu bar on a Mac, drawn in the window elsewhere.

  • Cursors drawn for each tool: the Pen's nib (with what a click will do), crosshairs for the Shape, Measure and Fill Angle tools, Direct Selection's hollow arrow, and a curved arrow at rotate corners.

  • Right-click menus on the canvas and the Objects list, styled like the tool flyouts: the stitch types with their icons, then the usual commands with their shortcuts.

  • Stays quick on big designs: stitches are planned once per change, reusing every object that didn't change (overlap removal too: moving one object redoes only the objects it overlaps); a design that takes more than 12 ms to plan plans in the background (the status bar says "Updating stitches…" and the last plan stays on screen meanwhile; when you drop a moved object its stitches move with it until the new plan lands). Dragging points or objects, and typing, preview without re-planning until you let go. The stitches live on the GPU: each color block's segments are uploaded once and drawn by a shader (thread shading and needle points included), so panning, zooming, dragging and the stitch player cost nothing per stitch on the CPU, whether the design has a thousand stitches or half a million. The Objects list lays out only the rows in view. An object whose stitches hit an internal error is left out with a warning in Issues rather than taking the plan down. For development: TL_PROFILE=1 prints each frame's sections to stderr, TL_NO_GPU=1 draws the stitches with the painter instead, and cargo test --release --features gui --bin zigzag-studio perf_bench -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1 times typing and dragging on a traced logo (examples/bench-grid.svg is a 213,000-stitch design for the studio itself).

  • Follows the system's light or dark appearance (ZIGZAG_THEME=light|dark overrides) and uses the San Francisco system font on a Mac.

  • Pick a stitch type per object: big buttons, the task bar, right-click, or F/S/R/C/X (Blanket and Manual from the Stitch panel). The preview re-plans live.

  • Layout, the Illustrator way: drag to move (Shift: 45° steps; Option: drag a copy). Handles resize freely (Shift keeps proportions, Option resizes from the center, drag past the far side to flip); just outside a corner rotates (Shift: 45°). Smart guides snap edges and centers to other objects and the hoop (View › Smart Guides, ⌘U). ⌘D is Transform Again: Option-drag a copy, then ⌘D for more at the same spacing. Hold Space to pan with any tool (a tap plays the stitch-out). The Transform panel has Illustrator's reference point: X/Y show the chosen point and W/H resize around it. Also rotate, flip, center in hoop, fit to hoop (artwork bigger than the hoop is scaled down to fit when you open or place it; Undo restores full size), ⌘C/⌘V, arrows nudge 0.5 mm (Shift 5 mm). Edits are saved as SVG transforms.

  • Groups work like Illustrator: a click or drag takes the whole group; double-click goes into it (the rest dims and a breadcrumb shows where you are), double-click again to go deeper; Esc or double-click on empty canvas comes back out. ⌘-click picks one object without going in. Layers (Illustrator's "Layer 1", Inkscape layers, Figma frames) aren't groups. Copy, paste and duplicate keep groups.

  • Type (T), as in VectorCraft and Illustrator: click where the text should go and type straight onto the canvas (Enter for a new line, Esc or a click elsewhere when done); click text, or between its letters, to edit it with the caret where you clicked (or double-click it with the Selection tool, which picks text anywhere in its box and shows it as a box, not its letters' points; delete every letter and finish, and the text is removed) (←/→, ↑/↓, Home/End and ⌘←/→ move it; Backspace and Delete remove either side; Shift with any of those, a drag, a double-click for a word, a triple-click or ⌘A for the lot selects text, which typing replaces and ⌘C/⌘X/⌘V copy, cut and paste); click a selected path to put text on it. The Lettering panel is a compact Character panel (hat text isn't long copy): font (with search), bold/italic, letter height, tracking, pair kerning (pick the pair, or Option+←/→ while typing kerns the pair at the caret), horizontal and vertical scale, case (as typed, UPPER, lower, Title), alignment and leading for two-line text, baseline (straight, arc over, arc under, or on a path with offset and flip), and the stitch type. The Type menu has Type on a Path, Change Case, Align and Create Outlines (⇧⌘O). Text is a shape like any other: Direct Selection, Round Corners, Simplify, Pathfinder and Clean Up all work on it (it quietly becomes plain paths at the first point-level edit, one undo step), and it saves as real SVG text until then.

  • Pen (P): draw filled shapes or lines with corners and curves, or place manual stitches one by one. Snaps to the grid when it's showing, else to smart guides.

  • Shapes (M, L, \): rectangles (with rounded corners), ellipses, polygons, stars and lines.

  • Measure, mm grid, needle points, First/Last, Group colors.

  • Open machine files (PES, PEC, DST, EXP, JEF) to view, resize and re-export them, and images to trace.

  • Settings per type: fill angle (with a drag-to-set angle tool, A), spacing, length, pull, underlay. Satin options: column vs border, stitch (satin, S-stitch, zig-zag), threads across the column, width, underlay passes, short stitches. Contour and ripple: rings or spiral. Cross-stitch: cell size. Tartan: the stripes (color and width each, mirrored), angle, row spacing. Run options: single or triple.

  • Sewing row in the Stitch panel: Start and End (click the outline; green and red markers you can drag), Trim and Stop after the object. Edit › Copy / Paste Stitch Settings carries one object's type and settings to others (each keeps its thread and start/end); Edit › Select Same Stitch Type; Object › Path › Reverse Direction sews a path from its other end.

  • Test swatches (Object › Test Swatches…): copies of the selection in a grid, one setting (spacing, length, pull compensation, satin width, fill angle) stepped from a value to another, each lettered with its value, to stitch out and compare on the real fabric.

  • View › Density Map tints where stitches pile up (yellow from 2.5 per mm², red at 4), and View › Sewing Order numbers the objects on the canvas.

  • Fabric preset, hoop, Remove overlaps and Cap order in the Document panel. Preview on your hat's color.

  • Issues list (status bar): problems link to the object. Satins show their rails on the canvas.

  • Sewing order: Earlier/Later. Stitch player (Space). Undo/redo everything.

  • Save (Ctrl/⌘ S) writes settings into the SVG; Export PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3/PEC/PEN or a worksheet (HTML: picture, size, time, every color stop with the nearest Brother and Janome thread); Send to Skitch.

  • Measuring and units. Measure (I) works like VectorCraft's: drag between two points to read the distance, angle, width and height. The ends snap to points, edges and the hoop (or to the grid when it's on), Shift keeps the line to 45°, and the reading stays until the next drag (Escape clears it). View › Units, or the unit menu in the status bar, shows sizes, positions, distances and the grid in millimeters, centimeters, inches, points or pixels (SVG pixels, 1/96 in, as files are read); it's remembered between launches. Any length field also takes a typed unit or a sum (1/4 in, 25.4mm, 10+5). The grid (⌘') follows the unit, inches in halves down to 1/32, and labels its major lines along the canvas's top and left edges from the hoop's center. Stitch settings (spacing, density, pull compensation) stay in millimeters.

  • Picks up where you left off. Quit (or crash) and reopen: the same files come back, every tab with any unsaved changes, the zoom and the selection, and the same tab in front. Changes are kept as you work (session.json and one recovery file per tab, recovery.svg, recovery-2.svg…, in ZigZag's settings folder (~/Library/Application Support/ZigZag), each written whole or not at all), never written into your file until you save. Opening the app with a file skips this. If the app went down while bringing a document back, the next launch keeps it aside as recovery-crashed.svg instead of trying again (and an unreadable one as recovery-unreadable.svg), and says so in the status bar. A job on the Skitch comes back too: the design last sent is kept (sent.json), the Skitch window reopens if it was open and reconnects, and once the machine reports that design its progress shows on it again (the machine keeps the design and where the needle is; Stop ends the job on both).

Agents (MCP)

The studio runs an MCP server on http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp (Streamable HTTP, localhost only, Origin-checked). Agents edit the live document you're looking at (the tab in front), and every call is one undo step.

MCP in the status bar (bottom right, next to the Skitch) shows whether agents can reach the studio: a gray dot while it waits, green once a client has connected, blue and pulsing while calls come in, red if the server couldn't start. Click it for the address, the commands to connect Claude Code and Claude Desktop (with Copy buttons), the clients that have connected, the recent tool calls (failed ones in red, with the error on hover) and the tools on offer.

Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http zigzag http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp

Claude Desktop / stdio clients (claude_desktop_config.json):

{ "mcpServers": { "zigzag": { "command": "/path/to/zigzag-mcp" } } }

zigzag-mcp forwards to the running studio. Use --port N if you changed it. With "args": ["--headless"] it works without the app open: the same tools on a document no one is watching (zigzag-studio --mcp-stdio), kept only when the agent saves or exports it.

Tools:

  • get_design, add_svg (place/scale artwork in mm), set_object, delete_object, move_object
  • transform_objects (size, scale, rotate, mirror, move), duplicate_objects
  • add_text, edit_text, list_fonts
  • set_document (fabric, hoop, overlaps, cap order, preview color), group_colors
  • render_preview (returns a PNG of the stitches), check_design, get_svg, select
  • open_file (SVG, machine file or image, in a tab of its own), list_documents, switch_document, new_document, undo, save, export (machine formats or html worksheet), send_to_skitch, machine_status
  • trace_image (PNG/JPEG logo → shapes, colors snapped to a thread chart), round_corners, simplify (VectorCraft's 0–100 levels, or Auto), clean_up
  • batch: several calls in one, all or nothing and one undo step; later steps can use earlier results ("$0.added.0.name")

Arguments a tool doesn't take are refused with the ones it does (a misspelt widht_mm isn't silently ignored), and each tool says whether it only reads.

Try asking: "Draw a 50 mm round badge with mountains and a sun for my thin cotton cap, check it, and show me the preview."

CLI

zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.pes -o logo.jef -o preview.png -o sheet.html [--fabric thin-cap] [--hat]
zigzag convert old.dst -o old.pes             # machine files convert too
zigzag convert logo.png -o logo.pes           # PNG/JPEG logos are traced first
zigzag info logo.svg                     # stats + checks
zigzag fabrics                           # list presets
zigzag skitch info | status              # needs --features ble
zigzag skitch send logo.svg --trace

Illustrator workflow

Export with File → Export → Export As → SVG (Styling: Presentation Attributes, Object IDs: Layer Names). Outline text, or it falls back to system fonts. Opening the ZigZag-saved SVG back in Illustrator keeps the settings in the layer names.

Name layers or objects to set their stitching. Illustrator's _x3D_-style escapes are decoded, and group settings apply to everything inside the group.

Token Meaning
fill satin run skip stitch type
a=45 fill angle (degrees)
s=0.3 row / zigzag spacing (mm)
l=3 max stitch length (mm)
pc=0.2 pull compensation (mm per side)
w=3 satin width (mm)
border satin along a filled shape's outline instead of across it
u=0 underlay off
ul=center+contour+zigzag satin underlay passes (ul=none)
ss=0 short stitches off
r=3 running passes (3 = bean)
contour blanket applique manual the other stitch types
split=7 satin auto-split length (mm); split=0 off
t=e8a33c thread color override
o=2 sewing order
stroke.… applies only to the stroke of an object that also has a fill, e.g. stroke.run

Example layer names: logo fill a=45 s=0.35, title satin, outline stroke.satin stroke.w=1.5.

Skitch over Bluetooth

The Skitch window (the toolbar's Send button or File › Send to Skitch…) runs the whole job, like a slicer's device page follows a print: the design on the left, what to do on the right, and the steps across the top (Connect · Home · Send · Trial · Sew · Done).

  • Connect and pair. It scans for the Skitch. The first time, hold the Skitch's Bluetooth button until it beeps, then Connect (or Try Again); if the computer asks to pair, accept. On a Mac the Skitch never appears in System Settings › Bluetooth (it's a Bluetooth LE device): it pairs when ZigZag connects. Allow ZigZag to use Bluetooth if macOS asks (Privacy & Security › Bluetooth). Close Artspira first: the Skitch talks to one app at a time.
  • Home. A machine just turned on asks to be homed (frame off, Accept, frame back on); the window shows the steps and moves on when it's done.
  • Send: the hoop with the design where it will sew: As Placed (where it sits in the studio's hoop, so you can put it high on a cap) or Centered; the threads to have ready, in sewing order, by Brother Embroidery name and number; a "before you sew" checklist; Send Design.
  • Trial run (Brother's name for it; on by default after sending): press Accept on the machine and the needle goes around the design's outline without sewing, so you can check it clears the frame's magnets, seams and the brim. Trial Again whenever you rehoop.
  • Sew: Start, then press Start on the machine. The picture shows what's sewn, faded where it hasn't been yet, with the needle and the thread on now; under it, a timeline of the threads with the needle's place. The side shows progress, time left, the thread on now and the next one, and at each thread change exactly which thread to put on. The canvas and the status bar follow along too.
  • Start / Pause / Stop. Start (or Resume, or Sew Again) readies the machine; Pause is the Skitch's own Start/Stop button (it can't be paused over Bluetooth); Stop ends the job, taking the design off the machine. While paused, drag along the timeline or step the needle by 1, 10 or 100 stitches or back to the thread's start, then Resume.
  • Errors say what they are and what to do (thread breaks, bobbin, needle plate, frame). After a thread break the needle goes back over the gap (6 stitches for the top thread, 2 for the bobbin, as Artspira does).
  • Minimize it (–) to keep working while it stitches: the canvas is your design again, and the machine's icon at the right of the status bar shows what it's doing and how far, with a small bar (click it to bring the window back). The window comes back by itself when the machine needs you: a thread change, an error, or the end.
  • The ••• menu also links to Brother's Skitch how-to videos (threading, the bobbin, the frame, a thread break, tension, cleaning).
  • The window's ••• menu can connect to a simulated machine, which does each step on the machine by itself, to try it all without a Skitch.

Agents can send_to_skitch and follow along with machine_status. The protocol was reverse-engineered (see NOTICE), so avoid firmware updates.

Working out undocumented commands

Thread tension isn't a Bluetooth setting on the Skitch: it's the tension dial on the machine. Speed is fixed (about 400 stitches a minute). The machine does report a block of settings, and Artspira has a settings screen, so two tools are here for working out what else it can do:

  • Settings bytes (in the Skitch window, under the machine's details): reads the settings block the machine reports. Read it, disconnect, change one setting in Artspira, close Artspira, reconnect and read again: the bytes that changed are marked. Every read is kept in skitch-settings.log beside the panel layout. On the command line: zigzag skitch settings --label "what changed" --log settings.log.
  • zigzag capture FILE lists the Skitch conversation in a Bluetooth recording of Artspira, by command name, with changed settings bytes in [brackets] (--all for the upload and polling too, --raw for every ATT operation). It reads both:
    • iPhone: install Apple's Bluetooth logging profile on the phone (developer.apple.com › Bug Reporting › Profiles and Logs), restart it, plug it into the Mac, and in PacketLogger (Apple's Additional Tools for Xcode) choose File › New iOS Trace; save the trace (.pklg).
    • Android: Developer options › Enable Bluetooth HCI snoop log, then adb bugreport and take btsnoop_hci.log from it.

Writing settings stays out of ZigZag until a layout is known and a write of the machine's own settings, unchanged, reads back the same.

Ink/Stitch parity

Checked against Ink/Stitch's features and tool docs:

Ink/Stitch ZigZag
Running, bean, manual stitch; satin column (two rails with rungs), E-stitch; tatami, contour, circular (spiral) fill ✓
Ripple, meander, cross-stitch and tartan fills; S-stitch, zigzag and multicolor satin ✓
Params per object with fabric-aware defaults; start/end commands; trim and stop commands ✓ (Stitch panel's Sewing row)
Auto-route (travel inside fills, underpath along the outline), Jump to Stroke ✓ (document's Connect gaps)
Simulator, stitch plan preview, density map, stacking-order labels ✓
Lettering (system fonts, arcs, text on a path, multi-line, case, scale), thread palettes, Match All, thread kits ✓ (Brother and Janome charts)
Duplicate params, select by type, flip satin direction, test swatches, cleanup, troubleshoot (Issues) ✓
Import stitch files and edit at stitch level; PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3/PEC ✓
Gradient fill, guided fill; redwork, cutwork; pre-digitized fonts; 60+ thread brands; PDF print not yet

Hatch parity

Checked against Wilcom Hatch's core feature set:

Hatch ZigZag
Tatami, satin, run/triple run, contour fill, blanket, appliqué, manual stitches ✓
Auto underlay, pull compensation, auto spacing, satin auto-split, short stitches ✓
Fabric settings that set densities and compensation ✓ (4 presets)
Lettering with TrueType fonts, straight, arc and path baselines, typed on the canvas ✓ (system fonts)
Select, move, resize, rotate, mirror, duplicate, copy/paste, align to hoop ✓
Digitize shapes and manual stitches by hand ✓ (pen tool)
Remove overlaps, color sequencing, re-order objects ✓
Stitch player, show needle points, grid, measure ✓
Open and save PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3 ✓ (VP3 write only)
Production worksheet ✓ (HTML)
Auto-digitize bitmaps ✓ (Image Trace: flat logos, posterized photos, centre lines)
Built-in embroidery fonts, monogramming, multi-hooping, motif/pattern fills, 3D foam not yet

Status

Verified:

  • 136 library tests, 153 editor/MCP tests (UI interactions via egui_kittest, a full agent workflow, a real HTTP JSON-RPC session, atomic batches, the Skitch flow against a simulated machine), with and without Bluetooth built in, plus the 222 tests of the vendored Image Trace.
  • Every writer (PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3) reads back through pyembroidery with identical stitch positions; our readers read pyembroidery-written files.
  • PEN output checked against hand-computed sequences.
  • Studio run on Mesa OpenGL and driven by an agent over MCP.

Not yet run against a real Skitch.

Screenshots and videos

Start the studio with ZIGZAG_CAPTURE=<folder> and ⌃⌥⌘S saves the window as a full-resolution PNG; ⌃⌥⌘R starts and stops recording it. packaging/media/encode.sh <folder>/take-001 demo turns a recording into demo.mp4 and demo.gif (needs ffmpeg).

Credits

See NOTICE, and THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md for the licenses of the libraries ZigZag is built from (regenerate it with packaging/licenses/generate.sh after changing dependencies). PES/PEC/DST layouts and the Brother palette are from pyembroidery (MIT). Image Trace is vendored from VectorCraft (MIT OR Apache-2.0), whose curve fitting, live corners, snap targets and colour difference were also ported (see vendor/README.md). Tatami, satin and short-stitch approaches follow Ink/Stitch.

item.title: Nintendo Takes Down Emulators and Firmware in Massive GitHub DMCA Sweep (300 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-takes-down-switch-emulators-and-mod-chip-firmware-in-massive-github-dmca-sweep, See on Hacker News

Nintendo has sent four DMCA takedown notices to GitHub targeting two Nintendo Switch emulators, Yuzu and Citron Neo, along with mod chip firmware.

This isn't the first time Nintendo has sent takedown notices to GitHub, and it's not even the first time it's tried to take down Yuzu, but the focus this time around seems to be on firmware for mod chips. This particular firmware had 144 repositories, all of which have been removed by GitHub and replaced by a DMCA takedown notice. Mod chips like Picofly can be soldered onto the Nintendo Switch's mainboard, and can be flashed with this firmware to circumvent Nintendo's copy protection.

GitHub has posted Nintendo's November 6 DMCA notice, which says, "The Nintendo Switch console and video games contain technological protection measures ('TPMs') that permit the Nintendo Switch console to interact only with legitimate Nintendo video game files. This process protects Nintendo’s copyright-protected video games, (...) by preventing users from playing pirated copies of Nintendo’s video games on the Nintendo Switch console and by preventing users from unlawfully copying and playing Nintendo’s video games on unauthorized devices."

A History of Every Nintendo Direct in the Switch Era and Beyond

However, while this takedown has effectively wiped out a ton of repositories with mod chip firmware, it seems like it's still being hosted elsewhere on the site, according to TorrentFreak. It's possible, though, that Nintendo isn't finished yet; back in 2024, Nintendo effectively took down 8,500 copies of Yuzu by issuing a takedown that targeted 12 different mirrors of the emulator.

This particular takedown also comes a few days after emulators were able to run the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on PC, so this could be a sign that Nintendo is winding up its lawyers to crack down on emulation once again.

If anything, emulation is a completely different beast in 2026 than it was even in 2024, thanks to the rise of AI. There's already been a wave of AI-made mashup mods that took over Twitter for a couple of weeks, and led Anthropic to coding in a lock to prevent Claude from outright copying games. Game developers have started cracking down on AI ports of games, too. Just last month Rockstar had to take down a browser version of GTA 5, and Bethesda took down an AI-generated Fallout New York game.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

item.title: ExcalidrawZ: Local Native Excalidraw on macOS/iOS (119 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/chocoford/ExcalidrawZ, See on Hacker News

A native Excalidraw client for macOS, iPadOS, and iOS. Powered by SwiftUI.

Excalidraw is an excellent drawing tool. ExcalidrawZ keeps the familiar Excalidraw canvas, then adds native file management, iCloud sync, history, export, AI assistance, MCP integration, and Apple-platform interaction details around it.

Download

Non-App Store version

  1. Download the latest .dmg from Releases.
  2. Open the .dmg and drag ExcalidrawZ into Applications.

Preview

Features

Native File Management

ExcalidrawZ manages drawings as real app documents instead of loose browser downloads.

  • Organize drawings with groups and custom file sorting.
  • Work with ExcalidrawZ library files, local folders, and temporary external files.
  • Open and edit .excalidraw, .excalidraw.png, and .excalidraw.svg files directly.
  • Sync app-managed files across macOS, iPadOS, and iOS with iCloud.
  • Keep file history checkpoints so important changes can be reviewed and restored.

File History

ExcalidrawZ records checkpoints for app-managed drawings, so you can review earlier versions and restore important work when needed.

Excalidraw Editing, Native Controls

The canvas remains compatible with Excalidraw while the surrounding app is built for Apple platforms.

  • Customize toolbar tool order; number shortcuts follow your configured order.
  • Use Apple Pencil on iPad, including familiar undo and redo gestures.
  • Use mouse and trackpad scroll and zoom gestures on iPad and iPhone.
  • Import PDFs and convert Mermaid diagrams into editable Excalidraw content.

Collaboration

Use Excalidraw collaboration when you want to draw with others.

AI Drawing Assistant

ExcalidrawZ includes an AI assistant designed for canvas work.

  • Ask AI to read, create, and revise drawings.
  • Attach images and let AI use visual context when needed.
  • Use proposal previews before applying AI-generated content to the real canvas.
  • Control whether each file is visible to AI.
  • Use AI from compact iPhone toolbars, iPad floating panels, or the macOS inspector.

MCP Services

ExcalidrawZ can expose the current app as an MCP server for compatible AI clients.

  • Basic mode provides the familiar excalidraw-mcp drawing workflow.
  • Optimized mode adds deeper ExcalidrawZ integration for current-file editing, file navigation, history, canvas inspection, export, library workflows, and math tools.
  • Connect local MCP clients through the app-hosted HTTP endpoint.

Math and Diagram Tools

ExcalidrawZ includes richer tools for technical drawings and study notes.

  • Insert LaTeX-rendered formulas.
  • Render function graphs with configurable axes and styles.
  • Use reusable math templates and AI-assisted formula generation.
  • Edit inserted math images later from the canvas.

Locked Files and AI Visibility

For sensitive drawings, ExcalidrawZ adds protection around both storage and AI access.

  • Lock files with local authentication.
  • Encrypt locked files and their checkpoints.
  • Use a Recovery Key for fallback access.
  • Keep locked content hidden from AI; AI can work through proposal canvases instead.
  • Use encrypted backups as an additional recovery path.

Share, Export, and Backup

ExcalidrawZ supports common export and sharing workflows.

  • Export images, editable Excalidraw files, and PDF.
  • Preserve editability when exporting .excalidraw.png and .excalidraw.svg.
  • Share through clipboard, files, and the system share sheet.
  • Archive app-managed files for backup.

Supported Formats

ExcalidrawZ can open, import, edit, or export common Excalidraw-related formats:

  • .excalidraw
  • .excalidraw.png
  • .excalidraw.svg
  • PDF import and export
  • image export

Contact

Welcome to my Discord server to share suggestions or report issues for ExcalidrawZ.

Development Guide

  • The Excalidraw core used by ExcalidrawZ is also open-source. You can find it here.

Signing configuration

Create Config/Overrides.xcconfig relative to the repository root, alongside Config/Project.xcconfig:

DEVELOPMENT_TEAM = YOUR_TEAM_ID
ICLOUD_CONTAINER = iCloud.com.yourname.ExcalidrawZ
APP_GROUP_IDENTIFIER = group.com.yourname.ExcalidrawZ

Replace these example values with identifiers registered to your Apple Developer team. The shared configuration leaves DEVELOPMENT_TEAM empty; set your team in the local overrides. The app and QuickLook extension must use the same App Group. All targets, including the extension and tests, inherit the team from Config/Project.xcconfig, which includes your local overrides. These overrides apply to all build configurations.

Runtime configuration

Create Config/Secrets.plist relative to the repository root. The project already references this file and includes it in both app targets' resources. The app's configuration loader stops with Unable to load Secrets.plist if the file is missing or invalid.

For local drawing development, this minimal configuration is sufficient:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>COLLAB_URL</key>
    <string>https://example.com</string>
</dict>
</plist>

COLLAB_URL must be a valid absolute URL. The example URL is a placeholder for local drawing work; to test collaboration, replace it with the URL of your deployed collaboration-enabled Excalidraw web client.

Optional string keys are ONEDRIVE_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_DRIVE_MACOS_CLIENT_ID, and GOOGLE_DRIVE_IOS_CLIENT_ID. Configure your own OAuth client IDs when developing the corresponding integrations.

Config/Overrides.xcconfig and Config/Secrets.plist are ignored by Git and should stay local.

item.title: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices (290 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/hyperionaidev/smolmaxxing/, See on Hacker News

Every device around you is more capable than it looks. TV boxes, old phones, single-board computers and routers all ship with CPUs, RAM and flash that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing is about unlocking that capability: finding the biggest language model each device can really run, then pushing it further with custom kernels, smarter memory use and weight streaming. Every claim is measured on the hardware itself.

Device #1 is a Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen): Amlogic S7D, 4× Cortex-A55 @ 2.5 GHz, 1.9 GB of RAM (about 1 GB usable), eMMC flash, Android 14, no root. On it, this repo runs models from 260 K to 16 B parameters:

  • Qwen3.5-0.8B: 16.8 tok/s (2.2× the stock 7.5; measured in the evening of 11-05, see §17).
  • Qwen3.5-2B: 7.7 tok/s in real chat. The box's speed drifts by ~10 % over a day, so every step is measured back to back: §16 gave +11 %, §17 another +7 %.
  • An 8B mixture-of-experts model (Moon-Beam-8B-A1B): 7.2 tok/s in real chat, its experts paged from flash on demand and prefetched one layer ahead (§19).
  • A dense 1-bit 8B model (Bonsai-8B): 5.2 tok/s in real chat, up from 1.2: fully resident in a "headless" mode plus a lookup-table kernel (§19).
  • A 16B mixture-of-experts model (Ling-mini-2.0): 5.1 tok/s in real chat, coherent over 600-word answers, the same expert pager applied unchanged (§20). Twice Moon-Beam's size, but not better per byte: bigger only helps on this box when the model is also better.
  • A dense 9B model: 0.27 tok/s, streaming most of its weights from flash.

Device #2 is a first-generation iPad Air (2013): Apple A7, 2 cores, NEON without dotprod, 1 GB of RAM, iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken, CPU only. A 13-year-old tablet runs a 1.7B-parameter model at 24-26 tok/s (18-22 in long chats), a 4B one at about 10 tok/s, an 8B mixture of experts at about 3.5 tok/s (5 with half its experts, at a quality cost), and a 16B one at 2.6-4.5 tok/s, with their experts paged from flash, from a chat page in its own Safari. See Results on device #2.

Every step is written up experiment by experiment in EXPERIMENT.md (E1-E160).

Devices

Device Status
Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen): Amlogic S7D, Cortex-A55, 2 GB ✅ done: 260K → 16B parameters, 8B at 5-7 tok/s, 16B at 5 tok/s
iPad Air (2013): Apple A7, 2 cores, 1 GB, iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken (ipad-air/) ✅ running: Bonsai-1.7B (1-bit) at 24-26 tok/s, 18-22 in long chats; Bonsai-4B at about 10 tok/s; Moon-Beam-8B-A1B (MoE) at about 3.5 tok/s; Ling-mini-2.0 (16B MoE) at 2.6-4.5 tok/s; CPU only
More TV boxes, phones, single-board computers, routers… 🔜 coming soon

The techniques aren't tied to one box. The 1-bit lookup-table kernel needs only base NEON, as the iPad shows; any ARM chip with dotprod gets the other kernels; and any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM can use the streaming engine.

Scoreboard

Class Best model First run → now (tok/s) Gain Bits/byte What got it there Download
0.8B Qwen3.5-0.8B 7.5 → 16.8 bench ×2.2 ≈1.00 all-Q4_K, padded 65K head, fp16 DeltaNet state HF
2B Qwen3.5-2B 0.1 → 7.7 chat ×77 0.909 all-Q4_K, padded 65K head, fused DeltaNet HF
4B Ternary-Bonsai-4B 2.2 → 4.3 chat ×2.0 ≈0.965 ternary weights in 2-bit fields, merged scales HF
8B dense Bonsai-8B (1-bit) 1.21 → 5.2 chat ×4.3 0.974 1-bit LUT kernel, fully resident in headless mode HF
8B MoE Moon-Beam-8B-A1B 1.87 → 7.2 chat ×3.9 0.996 Q2_K experts paged from flash, cache-aware routing, prefetch HF
9B Qwen3.5-9B 0.16 → 0.27 chat ×1.7 0.885 weight streaming plus its own MTP head rebuild (q9)
16B MoE Ling-mini-2.0 4.1 → 5.1 chat ×1.2 1.054 the Moon-Beam recipe, unchanged HF

"First run" is the first time each model ran on the box:

  • 0.8B: the stock Q4_K_M file.
  • 2B: the stock file, streamed from flash because it didn't fit in RAM. Its first build that fit ran at 4.8, so from there the gain is ×1.6.
  • 4B: the stock file, which thrashed.
  • 8B dense: the last 0.1 GB streamed from flash.
  • 8B MoE: the first expert-pager run, without routing bias.
  • 9B: streamed.
  • 16B: started on the Moon-Beam recipe, so its gain is small.

On this box, the 2B is the best speed-quality balance. Ling-mini-2.0 shows that bigger isn't automatically better: it is twice Moon-Beam's size, but scores worse per byte and runs slower.

What we built, grouped by the bottleneck it attacks (details and numbers in What's in here):

Bottleneck Innovations Biggest wins
Compute (in-order A55, 10 items) Q2_K and ternary repacks for vdotq_laneq, 1-bit bit planes, a 1-bit lookup-table kernel, ternary in 2-bit fields, Q8_0 attention with a skip threshold, fused Gated-DeltaNet, DeltaNet state read by id / fp16, the LM head on the fast kernel, guided matmul scheduling Q2_K 7.8 → 13.9 G weights/s; Bonsai-8B 3.77 → 5.1-5.4; 4B 3.2 → 4.3; long answers no longer halve the speed
RAM (~1 GB, 5 items) pruned LM head, lossless 1.875-bit ternary, headless mode, a fork-free memory guard, a repack cache on flash −0.2 to −0.5 GB per model; free RAM ~1,000 → ~1,300 MB; Bonsai-8B 1.2 → 3.6 before any kernel work
Flash (278 MB/s, 5 items) weight streaming with O_DIRECT, MTP speculation when flash-bound, expert pager, cache-aware routing, pre-gated prefetch 9B +69 %; expert misses 13 % → ~2 %; Moon-Beam 4.4 → 7.2
Output quality (2 items) a long-answer degeneration test, a repeat penalty of 1.15 over 256 tokens degenerate long answers 12/13 → 1/13

Results on device #1

Quality is English perplexity on a fixed 22 KB text, converted to bits per byte so models with different tokenizers compare fairly (lower is better). Speed is generation on the TV, measured either through llama-server with real chat requests ("chat") or with llama-bench ("bench").

Gemma 3 270M Q4_K_M 253 MB n/a 22 tok/s 73 tok/s
Qwen3.5-0.8B Q4_K_M (stock) 497 MB n/a 7.5 bench 28 tok/s
Qwen3.5-0.8B, all-Q4_K + 65K head 442 MiB (566 MB RSS) ≈1.00* 16.8 bench 33 tok/s best speed for its quality so far (§15-17)
Qwen3.5-2B, all-Q4_K + 65K head 0.99 GB 0.909 7.7 chat 17.8 the default: best overall (§11, §16, §17)

Moon-Beam-8B-A1B (MoE), Q2_K experts + 60K head 0.48 GB GGUF + 2.6 GB repack cache on flash, ~1.1 GB RSS 0.996 7.2 chat n/a fastest 8B: 128 experts, 6 used; expert pager, cache-aware routing, pre-gated prefetch, repeat penalty against long-answer loops (§19, headless mode)
Ling-mini-2.0 (MoE, 16.3 B), Q2_K experts + 60K head 0.47 GB GGUF + 5.3 GB repack cache on flash, ~1.13 GB RSS 1.054 5.1 chat n/a biggest model at a usable speed: 256 experts of 1 MB, 8 used, pool 43 per layer, bias 0.3 (§20)

Bonsai-8B, 1-bit + compact scales 0.84 GB + 0.12 GB streamed 0.991 1.21 chat (2.2 bench) 4.9 §14, before headless mode
Ternary-Bonsai-8B 0.89 GB + 0.80 GB streamed 0.919 0.31 bench 3.45 §14
Qwen3.5-9B UD-IQ2_XXS + MTP 0.63 GB + 1.6 GB streamed 0.885 0.16 chat, 0.27 with MTP 0.8 best quality; flash-bound (§14)

* measured on the pruned head's positions (1.3 % of tokens fall outside it), so not exactly comparable; the stock full-vocabulary Q4_0 file scores 1.024.

Other small models, stock files (screening, §15 E54):

Model Generation (bench) Prompt Bits/byte
LFM2.5-350M (QAD Q4_0) 23.7 tok/s 104 tok/s 1.805
LFM2-700M (Q4_0) 11.5 tok/s 52.8 tok/s 1.169
Qwen3-0.6B (Q8_0) 9.35 tok/s 50.6 tok/s 1.059
LFM2.5-1.2B (QAD Q4_0) 8.3 tok/s 31.6 tok/s 1.133
Llama 3.2 1B (Q4_0) 7.0 tok/s 29.5 tok/s 0.998
Ternary-Bonsai-2-2B (Q2_0) 5.9 tok/s 15.8 tok/s 1.124
Gemma 3 1B (Q4_K_M) 5.7 tok/s 11.1 tok/s 1.260
Granite 4.0 H 1B (Q4_0, ~1.5 B) too big as shipped 0.916
↳ rebuilt: all-Q4_K, Q8_0 embedding, 48K head (E62) 5.29 tok/s (fits only after freeing RAM, 950 MB RSS) 0.919
LFM3-1.7B (QAD Q4_0) doesn't fit

Granite 4.0 H 1B was the one model close to the 2B's quality. Rebuilt our way (E62), it runs at 5.29 tok/s, below the 2B's 6.55 at slightly lower quality: it carries about twice the 0.8B's weight bytes per token.

Physics of the box: one process can hold ~0.96 GB before Android starts killing things (~1.15 GB in headless mode, with the launchers and Google services force-stopped), and flash reads top out at 278 MB/s, with a lone ~1 MB random read costing ~6 ms. A model that has to stream X MB per token can never beat 278 / X tokens per second. That, not the CPU, is what limits everything above 2B, and why a mixture-of-experts model, which touches ~1 B of its 8 B weights per token, is the way past it.

10 tok/s at 8 B? Measured, not guessed (E98): Moon-Beam reaches 10.4 tok/s with 2 experts per token, but the text turns to gibberish; the best coherent setting is ~7-8 tok/s. Dense Qwen3-8B is Bonsai-8B at 1 bit, and the smallest Qwen MoE (35B-A3B) touches 3× Moon-Beam's weights per token.

Results on device #2

A 2013 iPad Air: Apple A7, 2 cores, NEON without dotprod, 1 GB of RAM, iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken with Amethyst. Everything runs on the CPU with 2 threads and a 1,024-token context, cross-compiled from a Mac. The write-up is §21 of EXPERIMENT.md, and build steps are in ipad-air/README.md.

Model File Generation (tok/s) Peak RSS Fixed three-question test
Bonsai-1.7B Q1_0 (1-bit) 237 MiB 23.7-25.8, 18-22 through long chats 605 MB all three right, and writes correct code: the one to use
Bonsai-4B Q1_0 (1-bit), -c 512 -b 64 546 MiB 9.4-11.4, 9.2-10.3 through long chats; as a server, iOS resets it within minutes 615-682 MB right on France, tides mostly right, fails recall every run; better per byte (1.073 vs 1.158 bits/byte)
Moon-Beam-8B-A1B (MoE, Q2_K experts), expert pager, -c 512 -b 64 2.6 GiB (474 MB mapped) 3.5-3.6 on longer answers; 4.9-5.1 with --experts 4 (+27 % perplexity) ~600-625 MB all three right; a session model, too big for the always-on server
SmolLM2-360M-Instruct Q4_K_M 258 MiB 10.9-12.5 269-316 MB all three right; the lightest good option
Gemma 3 270M-it Q4_K_M 241 MiB 15.4-19.0 248-294 MB wrong on tides, empty reply on recall
SmolLM2-135M-Instruct Q4_K_M 101 MB 18.6-29.3 141 MB right on France and recall, weak on tides
Qwen3.5-0.8B Q4_K_M 508 MiB about 0.2 506 MB thrashes the page cache, stopped by hand

Only the Bonsai and Moon-Beam rows were measured on the latest build. The other rows predate the attention and sampler work below.

Class Best model First run → now (tok/s) Gain What got it there
1.7B Bonsai-1.7B (1-bit) 2.75 → 23.7-25.8 ×8.6 multiplication-free and lookup-table 1-bit kernels without dotprod, the LM head on the fast kernel, row-order attention with pruning, a one-pass sampler
4B Bonsai-4B (1-bit) 9.4-11.4 the 1.7B's kernels, attention for 4 q heads per K head, -c 512 -b 64 to stay under the ~700 MB ceiling
8B dense Bonsai-8B (1-bit) 0.08 doesn't fit in RAM; most of the file is re-read from flash every token
8B MoE Moon-Beam-8B-A1B can't load → 1.6 → 3.5 (5.0 with 4 experts, +27 % perplexity) ×2.2 expert pager, Q2_K lookup-table kernel, prefetch, cache bias 0.03, frequency-based eviction
16B MoE Ling-mini-2.0 can't load → 2.6 (3.3 at +2.6 %, 4.5 with bias 0.3) new the Moon-Beam recipe, and a model file assembled over HTTP and streamed straight to the iPad

"Can't load": iOS 12 lets a process map at most about 1.7 GB, so stock llama.cpp fails on the 2.6 and 5.5 GB files before running a token. "First run" for Moon-Beam is the first expert-pager run (pool 8, no bias).

What we built on the iPad, grouped by the bottleneck it attacks:

Bottleneck Innovations Biggest wins
Compute (2-core A7, no dotprod, 6 items) a multiplication-free 1-bit kernel, the TV's 1-bit lookup-table kernel ported to base NEON, a lookup-table copy of the tied LM head, row-order attention with pruning (2 or 4 q heads per K head), a one-pass sampler with a 40-entry heap, a Q2_K lookup-table kernel for experts Bonsai-1.7B 2.75 → 3.45 → ~11 → 23.7-25.8 tok/s; sampling 3 → 0.23 ms per token; Moon-Beam 2.94 → 3.06 from the Q2_K kernel alone
Address space and RAM (~1.7 GB mappable, ~700 MB usable, 4 items) an expert pager that maps only the non-expert part (experts-last files), pruned LM heads for bailingmoe2 and bailingmoe3, small batches (-c 512 -b 64), std::filesystem compiled out for iOS 12 8B and 16B MoE models load at all, in 556-625 MB; Bonsai-4B fits
Flash (~260 MB/s, 5 items) uncached pread with 4 readers, reads queued by when they're needed, pre-gated prefetch, cache-aware routing bias, decayed-frequency eviction Moon-Beam 1.6 → 3.5 tok/s at no quality cost; misses 42 % → 38 % from eviction alone
Tooling (5 items) an op profiler with page-fault counts, an expert trace and cache simulator, on-device perplexity (tinyppl), model assembly over HTTP range requests, a bench that kills orphaned runs found the LM head that never reached the fast kernel (45 of 72 ms); ruled out the soft-fault theory; built a 5.5 GB model with 1.4 GB of Mac disk

How Bonsai-1.7B got from 2.75 to about 25 tok/s (same model file throughout):

Step tok/s What changed
Stock llama.cpp, 2 threads 2.75 emulates dotprod with widening multiplies
Multiplication-free NEON kernel 3.45 weights are ±1, so no multiply is needed; output identical
Lookup-table kernel from device #1, ported to base NEON about 11 its dotprod requirement turned out to be only an assumption
The output head on that kernel 18-22 151,669 rows isn't a multiple of 32, so the tied head had never reached it: 45 of 72 ms per token
Row-order attention with pruning, and a sampler that doesn't sort the vocabulary 23.7-25.8 the KV cache stores all heads of a row side by side, so one head at a time missed the cache constantly

In long chats (400-token answers), the three turns went from 15.4 / 7.6 / 8.2 to 21.8 / 17.9 / 18.4 tok/s through the attention work alone. The pruning threshold that holds long chats above 17 costs +0.42 % perplexity at 1,024 tokens of context, near the ±0.3 % noise floor; GGML_FA_EPS=0.0001 trades that back for about 15 tok/s.

An 8B model, through an expert pager. iOS 12 caps a process at about 1.7 GB of mapped address space (1.3 GB for the web server's user), so Moon-Beam-8B's 2.6 GB file can't even be mapped, and keeping fewer experts to make it fit more than doubles its perplexity (§21.7). Dense Bonsai-8B runs at 0.08 tok/s from flash. So the model file is rewritten with its experts last, only the 474 MB before them is mapped, and each layer keeps 14 experts in RAM, reading the others from flash with pread when the router picks them. Results match the unpaged model exactly. A small routing bias toward experts already in RAM (+0.3 % perplexity, inside the noise) brought it to 2.4-2.8 tok/s in about 600 MB (§21.8). Round 2 (§21.9) queues flash reads by when they're needed, prefetches the next layer's likely experts, and runs the experts through a lookup-table kernel for Q2_K: 3.4 tok/s, 40× the dense 8B, at +0.7 % perplexity on the full eval text. The flash is still the limit: each token reads about 53 MB at 266 MB/s. Wiring weights in RAM kernel-panicked the iPad, like a pool of 16 did before. Round 3 (§21.10) evicts by decayed use frequency instead of recency, for 3.5 tok/s at no quality cost. 5 tok/s takes 4 experts per token instead of 8 (+27 % perplexity); choosing the count per token adaptively turned out no better than a fixed count. A 16B model (§21.11): Ling-mini-2.0, 16.3B parameters with 256 small experts per layer, runs through the same pager at 2.6 tok/s with unchanged routing, 3.3 at +2.6 % perplexity and 4.5 with a strong cache bias, in under 580 MB. Its 5.5 GB file was assembled from two published quantizations over HTTP range requests and streamed straight to the iPad, since the Mac had no room for it. It is twice Moon-Beam's size at the same speed, but not a better model (+3 % perplexity).

Limits worth knowing. Bonsai is a 1-bit model and still gets facts wrong (in one test it called Mercury the closest planet to Earth). About 700 MB is the practical memory ceiling: 1-bit weights don't compress, so iOS starts killing processes past it, which is why the 4B needs a 512-token context. The jailbreak doesn't survive a reboot. The fast output head adds 2-3 s to the first prompt after each launch.

What's in here

Kernels for Cortex-A55 (ARMv8.2 dotprod, no i8mm), as a patch on llama.cpp v0.8.0, each with an exactness test against a scalar reference:

Kernel Before → after Where
Q2_K, repacked 8 rows × 4 bytes for vdotq_laneq (upstream repacks Q2_K only on x86 / RISC-V) 7.8 → 13.9 G weights/s; generation +41 %, prompt 2.4× E34
TQ1_0 / TQ2_0 ternary, repacked 9.5 → 14.4 / 11.9 → 19.1 G weights/s E38
Ternary Q2_0 → lossless 1.875 bits/weight in RAM (base-3 packing that keeps the per-64 scales) Ternary-Bonsai-4B from "thrashes" to 3.2 tok/s E39, E42
Q1_0 bit planes: vtst turns a bit plane straight into a mask for vdot, no table lookups; 8-bit row-affine scales (−5.6 %, 0.07 % error) Bonsai-4B 3.02 → 4.22 tok/s; Bonsai-8B fits in 0.96 GB E44, E52
Fused Gated-DeltaNet step with direct state write (Qwen3.5) 2B 6.0 → 6.3-6.7 tok/s E28
DeltaNet state read in place by id instead of a 1 MB/layer gather every token; fp16 state (LLAMA_STATE_F16=1, on by default in the UI) 0.8B 11.9 → 12.9 tok/s; 2B +2.5 % for +0.15 % perplexity E56, E61, E65
The LM head on the fast kernel: the 65,668-row head was never repacked (ggml repacks only row counts divisible by 8), so 4 token rows were added; embedding rows are then rebuilt from the repacked head (inverse 8-row interleave) instead of read from flash; the one-token DeltaNet conv step fused from 4 nodes into one NEON op 2B +7 % (bench and chat); 0.8B +9.5 % E69-E72
Ternary weights in 2-bit fields, with scales merged per 128: on the in-order A55, one base-3 digit costs ~5 NEON ops per 16 weights and a 2-bit field costs 2, so spending 13 % more RAM buys speed. Merging adjacent scales costs +0.18 % perplexity Ternary-Bonsai-4B 3.2 → 4.3 tok/s in chat, prompt 7.0 → 9.6 E76, E77
1-bit lookup-table kernel (Four-Russians / T-MAC style): 32 rows per group, one 16-entry table per 4 activations built straight from the float activations, ~8 NEON ops + 2 loads per 128 multiply-adds vs 16 + 4 Bonsai-8B 3.77 → 5.1-5.4 tok/s (with E82, E88) E81
Q8_0 attention with a threshold: all K dots first with sdot, so the softmax maximum is known up front, then expf and V work skipped for rows below max + ln(1e-4) a 1,000-token answer no longer halves the speed (2.50 → ~4 tok/s at the end) E86
Guided matmul scheduling: each thread grabs remaining / (2 × threads) rows, so a slow or preempted thread leaves a short tail instead of ~28 ms per token of idle cores; single-row element-wise ops split by columns (ggml left them all on thread 0) 2B 6.26 → 6.54 tok/s; 0.8B +1.4 % E63, E64

Memory tricks:

  • Pruned LM head: keep only the ~49-66 K most useful vocabulary rows, chosen by token frequency on English, code and 7 other languages. The other logits are scattered to −inf. Saves 0.2-0.5 GB and misses ~1 % of English tokens.
  • Repack cache on flash (GGML_REPACK_CACHE): repacked weights are written to a file once and mapped afterwards. Models load in seconds.

Headless mode (tools/tv-llm-mode.sh on|off): a small foreground activity, then the launchers, Google services and other heavy apps are force-stopped, and svc power stayon keeps the animated screensaver (17 % of a core) away. Nothing persistent except stay-awake, which off restores. MemAvailable ~1000 → ~1300 MB. A fork-free guard (tools/tv-watch.c) replaced a shell loop that started ~25 processes a second and cost 10 % of the speed.

Expert pager for mixture-of-experts models (ggml-cpu/moe-pager-tv.inc):

  • Experts live on flash: each expert tensor is overlaid with empty anonymous memory, and right after a layer's routing the missing experts are read with parallel O_DIRECT straight into their own addresses; a per-layer LRU pool (43 of 128 experts) keeps the rest. Kernels see an ordinary tensor. The GGUF's own expert bytes are hole-punched once the repack cache holds them, so the model costs one copy of its weights on flash.
  • Cache-aware routing (GGML_MOE_BIAS): a small bonus for experts already in RAM cuts misses from 13 % to ~2 % for a measured quality cost (arXiv 2412.00099 has the idea on other models). Fewer experts per token (LLAMA_MOE_USED=6) is the other dial.
  • Warm start from a list of each layer's most used experts, and pre-gated prefetch: layer L+2's router applied to layer L's hidden state, predicting what the router will actually pick (sigmoid, the model's own selection bias and the cache bonus), loads ~60 % of misses before they are needed.
  • Why answers looped, and the fix: 2-bit experts break long-form coherence after ~250-300 words, and routing bias amplifies it. DRY sampling only hides it (the model paraphrases its loop); a repeat penalty of 1.15 over 256 tokens brings degenerate long answers from 12/13 to 1/13 on the TV (E99, E100).

Weight streaming for models bigger than RAM (ggml-cpu/stream-tv.inc):

  • What stays in RAM: a chosen part of the weights stays resident. The rest lives in "stream zones".
  • Prefetch: a hook on every matmul records the order the weights are used. Reader threads then fetch zone weights ahead of time with parallel 8 MB O_DIRECT reads straight into the weights' own addresses, at the flash's full 278 MB/s.
  • Correctness: every compute thread waits until its weight is completely loaded, so a wrong prediction costs time, never correctness.
  • Drop-behind: each zone weight is freed right after use.
  • Verify mode: GGML_STREAM_VERIFY=1 compares every streamed tensor with the file. It found two silent-corruption bugs, which are fixed and documented in E48 and E50.
  • Speculative decoding: with the model's own MTP head, verifying 2 tokens costs about one pass over the weights when the pass is flash-bound, so it pays off (+69 %). On the in-RAM 2B it lost (E31).

Profiling (env switches in the patch): GGML_OPPROF=1 per-op table, GGML_OPPROF=2 a node-by-node, per-thread trace of one graph (tools/optrace.py), LLAMA_UBATCH_PROF / GGML_CPU_PROF phase timings. They showed where a small model's time really goes (E57): ~71 % Q4_K matmuls, and only ~2 ms per token of barriers and scheduling.

Tooling:

  • Streaming GGUF rewriter: adds a pruned head, extra tensors and metadata in one sequential pass, so Hugging Face → Mac → TV pipelines never store the model on the Mac.
  • MTP fetcher: range-reads only the MTP tensors from safetensors.
  • Memory guard: wraps every heavy run on the TV.
  • Benchmark and perplexity harnesses, a model screener that streams any Hugging Face GGUF to the TV and scores it (tools/screen-small.sh), and a live token-stream web UI.

Quick start

You need: the TV box (or another ARMv8.2 Android device) with network ADB, adb, zig (for static aarch64 musl builds), cmake + ninja, python3, and uv (for numpy).

export ADB_SERIAL=<tv-ip>:5555          # every script talks to the box through this
adb connect $ADB_SERIAL

# 1. llama.cpp v0.8.0 + the patch, cross-compiled for the TV
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp third_party/llama.cpp
cd third_party/llama.cpp && git checkout 8642541 && git apply ../../patches/llama.cpp-v0.8.0-tvbox.patch
cmake -S . -B build-tv -G Ninja -DCMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME=Linux -DCMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR=aarch64 \

Lessons

  • On this box the 2B at 4 bits beats every bigger model at 1-2 bits. Post-training quantization below ~2.5 bits breaks normal models (E22, E23, E35). Models trained for 1-bit or ternary hold up, but at 4-8 B they don't fit without streaming.
  • Past RAM, flash bandwidth sets the speed. The kernel's LRU is the worst possible policy for a cyclic scan bigger than the cache: it re-reads everything every token. Keep a fixed resident set and stream the rest yourself.
  • Batching is free when you are flash-bound. Prompts and speculative verification cost about one weight pass, whatever their size.
  • Measure, then verify. Two streaming bugs gave plausible speeds and wrong numbers; only comparing tensors with the file, and perplexity with a Mac reference, caught them.
  • Small models are mostly vocabulary. Qwen3.5-0.8B's 248K-row head is a third of its weights; pruning it to 65K rows plus all-Q4_K took it from 7.5 to 12.1 tok/s (E55). Small models also lose more to 4 bits (+7 % perplexity vs +2.3 % for the 2B).
  • Simulate before you write a kernel. Activation sparsity (E58) and a low-rank head (E60) both looked promising on paper; a quality simulation on the Mac killed each in under an hour.
  • On an in-order core, count NEON ops as well as bytes. Tighter packing saved 20 % of the bytes and cost 2.5× the ops; undoing it made the 4B 33 % faster in chat (E76, E77). The 4-bit kernel is the opposite case, limited by RAM (E27), so the trick does not help the 2B or 0.8B.
  • Check that every big matrix reaches the fast kernel. The 2B's head (65,668 rows, ~10 % of each token's weights) silently ran on the generic kernel for weeks because ggml only repacks row counts divisible by 8; four extra rows gave +5.8 % (E71, E72). The load log's repack buffer size gives it away.
  • Most of the RAM was Android's, not the model's. Force-stopping the launchers and Google services for the duration (nothing persistent) let Bonsai-8B sit fully in RAM: 1.2 → 3.6 tok/s before any kernel work (E80). An animated screensaver and a guard that forked 25 times a second each cost another 10-15 % (E82, E88).
  • For a mixture-of-experts model the flash is a cache miss, not a stream. A ~6 ms miss per expert means the pool hit rate decides the speed; routing toward cached experts and prefetching what the next router will pick turned 4.4 into 7.2 tok/s.
  • Perplexity can't see loops. It scores one token at a time on clean text; the 2-bit model scored fine and still fell into loops in 12 of 13 long answers. Score long free-running generations too (tools/loop_stats.py), and compare models with different tokenizers in bits per byte, never in perplexity.
  • Past 9B, count resident bytes, not parameters. The ceiling for a mixture-of-experts model here is the non-expert weights that must stay in RAM plus a useful expert pool. Ling-mini-2.0 (16B) keeps 279 MB resident and runs at 5 tok/s; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B would need ~870 MB before caching a single expert (§20).
  • Guard the box. After two early kernel panics, every heavy run goes through a wrapper that kills it below 180 MB of free memory.
